questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,i]\times \{i\}.$ Which of the following represents ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,0.5]\times \{0.5\}=\{(k,0.5)\,:\,k\in [0,0.5]\}.
$$

This represents a horizontal line segment from the point $(0,0.5)$ to the point $(0.5,0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/7587daeaea45c5ef3449ecb676133c60bbedb7819308783bac835f3ae9c6883c.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,i]\times \{i\}=\{(k,i)\,:\,k\in [0,i]\}
$$

is the horizontal line segment from the point $(0,i)$ to the point $(i,i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/b926204a3d58b25889f1c79dd0f65c1ea990c67bc88e869004396a77970e8dd4.png)

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following triangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/4a81de1a698eedf6a636d66b68a7c62efa69d1d026a961ae97ab5ecc2ef9828d.png)

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $-1$ or $1.$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in \{-1,1\}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/3ed05ffc58aad1a6c75e7862c1175f497fb14870e6650cc6c4ce01c3df091d8b.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/0f57920b2532177b0d64ac3dc95feb6a476bb385112d736d702895862e7de2b2.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/075454dae9ed36967a70537cdf3a3f59931cdd81671ff4059658d2e0df438898.png)

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=Z\times R$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=Z\times R
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in Z,\,y\in R\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(-1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/3fdfed680e3fb46adbe8a70aac86682aacb85d43e0675923f87658635fc89a1e.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/7fbda500ecca7e18c9db9939ad78d4dcc6bf488bc7fc4de1137e764ce21a0254.png)

We can create the subsets $…,{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}… \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $Z\times R$ as the set of vertical lines shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/4535a7c6aa7fe8f358d3463b4654c735e53df373d1001916dc035290ca54f969.png)

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,2]\times [-0.5,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-0.5,0]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-0.5),$ and $(0,-0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/5837864bfcc40e680cf62b43c0e3d145ba05b1f25e1ccae2f4788902d030d927.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-i,0]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-i),$ and $(0,-i).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/f0c20436f03db4b0003d087827cefbd76506af423da3f0a3042082b5afeb4b58.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $[0,2]\times \{0\}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/236d10f31265b400036e1ddeafa122991bcae1ea878af8b300003fb11acfa85b.png)

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}$ in the Cartesian plane?
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $-1$ or $1.$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in \{-1,1\}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/3ed05ffc58aad1a6c75e7862c1175f497fb14870e6650cc6c4ce01c3df091d8b.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/0f57920b2532177b0d64ac3dc95feb6a476bb385112d736d702895862e7de2b2.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/075454dae9ed36967a70537cdf3a3f59931cdd81671ff4059658d2e0df438898.png)

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,2]\times [-0.5,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-0.5,0]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-0.5),$ and $(0,-0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/5837864bfcc40e680cf62b43c0e3d145ba05b1f25e1ccae2f4788902d030d927.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-i,0]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-i),$ and $(0,-i).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/f0c20436f03db4b0003d087827cefbd76506af423da3f0a3042082b5afeb4b58.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $[0,2]\times \{0\}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/236d10f31265b400036e1ddeafa122991bcae1ea878af8b300003fb11acfa85b.png)

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,2]\times [-0.5,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-0.5,0]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-0.5),$ and $(0,-0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/5837864bfcc40e680cf62b43c0e3d145ba05b1f25e1ccae2f4788902d030d927.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-i,0]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-i),$ and $(0,-i).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167512/assets/f0c20436f03db4b0003d087827cefbd76506af423da3f0a3042082b5afeb4b58.png)

In general, Xi=[0,2]×[−i,0]={(a,b):a∈[0,2],b∈[−i,0]} is the rectangle whose vertices are at (0,0), (2,0), (2,−i), and (0,−i).

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment [0,2]×{0}:

solution.reasoning: Because 0 belongs to I, the intersection is contained in X_0=[0,2]×{0}. Every point of X_0 also belongs to every X_i, since 0 lies in [-i,0]. Thus the intersection is exactly the closed horizontal segment from (0,0) to (2,0), shown in option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $13$ and $8,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $13,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=13\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{13}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{13}.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $7,$ $3,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $7,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=7\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{7}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{7}.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{3},$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={6}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={6}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=6.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=6.$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{5},$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=10,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={10}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={10}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=10.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=10.$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/6be1f51600ae7b42ad0c4c8f67eb8f3ba3570606ec4e3e5e75c65df397aab060.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=7={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=5={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=7$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/f9b7a55ee1b8d3327ae9da740feaafde459daaee4e42a27cf26fd0ac8e63f20b.png)

A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $36$ of ${A}^{T}A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=6={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={6}^{2}=36,$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=2={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={2}^{2}=4.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=36$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{1}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/57368434b3025dc777c5be725da43e365dfd8ef3c47049570c0ecb13f2baf035.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=9={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=4={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere
canonical_examples.problem: A $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Given that the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are $7, 2,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $7,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 7
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\}  = \sqrt{7}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{7}.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values
canonical_examples.problem: A $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are $\sigma_1=4,$ $\sigma_2=2,$ and $\sigma_3 = 0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is $\sigma_1=4,$ the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ must be $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=4^2.$ So, we obtain that

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 4^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sigma_1=4.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/094b6043b9cce7f3ac2a7cc32fa53785d3fbf5b490ce853474f89bb4afa8291a.png)

A $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ are unit eigenvectors of $A^TA,$ find an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $36$ of $A^T A?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A^T A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n.
$$

Then,

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

- $\cdots$

In our example, we see that

- $||A\mathbf v_1|| = 8 = \sigma_1,$ which means that $\lambda_1 = 8^2 = 64,$ and

- $||A\mathbf v_2|| = 6 = \sigma_2,$ which means that $\lambda_2 = 6^2 = 36.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = 36$ of $A^T A$ is $\mathbf{v}_2.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Problems Regarding the Image of the Unit Eigenvectors of a Quadratic Form

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$

tutorials.content:
Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$

tutorials.name: The Singular Values of a Matrix
tutorials.problem:
Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix. Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$

- $\sigma_3 = \sqrt{\lambda_3}$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$

We usually list the singular values in *decreasing* order. 

Now, we know that $A^TA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable. Therefore, if

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

is an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A^T}{A}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,
$$

then it can be shown that

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_n.$

Furthermore:

- $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_1$

- $\sigma_2$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_2$

- $\sigma_3$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1$ *and* $\mathbf v_2,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_3$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_{n-1},$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_n$

Let's take a look at a concrete example.

tutorials.name: Associating Singular Values With an Ellipse's Principal Axes
tutorials.problem:
We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/9c11e176876a767543250d5b18038cae7b14a36a692a6f14474da6b4312a48b9.svg)

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/7c44b67b766ea8385f4d7780523ee560bd3e215a0cee42db9baf208da471ccdd.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

 

Note that our ellipse's semi-major and semi-minor axes are $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 =2,$ respectively.

tutorials.content:
We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/9c11e176876a767543250d5b18038cae7b14a36a692a6f14474da6b4312a48b9.svg)

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/7c44b67b766ea8385f4d7780523ee560bd3e215a0cee42db9baf208da471ccdd.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

 

Note that our ellipse's semi-major and semi-minor axes are $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 =2,$ respectively.

tutorial.problem:
Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/575b639f926dd7585dcc4ceed2a2c19c08b4260919f6b772202d4d8415170787.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$

\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$

tutorial.name: The Singular Values of a Matrix
tutorial.problem:
Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix. Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$

- $\sigma_3 = \sqrt{\lambda_3}$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$

We usually list the singular values in *decreasing* order. 

Now, we know that $A^TA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable. Therefore, if

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

is an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A^T}{A}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,
$$

then it can be shown that

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_n.$

Furthermore:

- $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_1$

- $\sigma_2$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_2$

- $\sigma_3$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1$ *and* $\mathbf v_2,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_3$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_{n-1},$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_n$

Let's take a look at a concrete example.

tutorial.content:
We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/d0bc1a894bd4becb168f55f5ac4f97ee91451add907911034beef7b7728a14d2.svg)

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/ca86ebe2257e15723c0a9704bd27f1b22c12b532b9f09ee844609674d2bebf5e.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

 

Note that our ellipse's semi-major and semi-minor axes are $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 =2,$ respectively.
tutorial.title: Associating Singular Values With an Ellipse's Principal Axes

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is $\sigma_1=4,$ the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ must be $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=4^2.$ So, we obtain that

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 4^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sigma_1=4.$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={6}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={6}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=6.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=6.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=6 and σ2=23, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
23
b
6
c
3
d
12
e
6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=6, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=62. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=62⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=6.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=6.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=5,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={5}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={5}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=5.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=5.$

The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={7}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=7.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=7.$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A^T A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n.
$$

Then,

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

- $\cdots$

In our example, we see that

- $||A\mathbf v_1|| = 8 = \sigma_1,$ which means that $\lambda_1 = 8^2 = 64,$ and

- $||A\mathbf v_2|| = 6 = \sigma_2,$ which means that $\lambda_2 = 6^2 = 36.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = 36$ of $A^T A$ is $\mathbf{v}_2.$

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

  • ||Av1||=6=σ1, which means that λ1=62=36, and

  • ||Av2||=2=σ2, which means that λ2=22=4.

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ1=36 of ATA is v1.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/57368434b3025dc777c5be725da43e365dfd8ef3c47049570c0ecb13f2baf035.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=9={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=4={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$

Question 15
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
9 and 4
b
18 and 8
c
3 and 2
d
v1 and v1
e
9v1 and 4v1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=9=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=4=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=9 and σ2=4.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $13$ and $8,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
question.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $13,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=13\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{13}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{13}.$

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the eigenvalues of ATA are 13 and 8, find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.

a
22
b
13
c
23
d
13
e
8
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

Since the largest eigenvalue of ATA is 13, we obtain

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=13⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=13.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is 13.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $13,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=13\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{13}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{13}.$

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the eigenvalues of ATA are 13 and 8, find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.

a
22
b
13
c
23
d
13
e
8

EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

Since the largest eigenvalue of ATA is 13, we obtain

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=13⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=13.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $12,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=12\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $2\sqrt{3}.$

Question 2
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the eigenvalues of ATA are 12 and 7, find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.

a
7
b
43
c
3
d
12
e
23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

Since the largest eigenvalue of ATA is 12, we obtain

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=12⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=12=23.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is 23.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $15,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=15\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{15}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{15}.$

The matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=15⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=15.

question.html:
Question 5
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the eigenvalues of ATA are 12, 9, and 0, find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.

a
43
b
12
c
9
d
23
e
0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

Since the largest eigenvalue of ATA is 12, we obtain

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=12⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=12=23.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is 23.

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{3},$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
question.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={6}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={6}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=6.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=6.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=6 and σ2=23, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
23
b
6
c
3
d
12
e
6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=6, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=62. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=62⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=6.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=6.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{3},$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
feedback.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={6}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={6}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=6.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=6.$

Question 7

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=5, σ2=2, and σ3=0, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
10
b
5
c
5
d
52
e
10
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=5, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=52. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=52⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=5.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=5.

Question 8
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=10 and σ2=25, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
50
b
10
c
25
d
100
e
10
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=10, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=102. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=102⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=10.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=10.

question.html:
Question 9
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=6, σ2=4, and σ3=0, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
4
b
36
c
6
d
6
e
2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=6, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=62. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=62⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=6.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=6.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem: A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ ${\sigma }_{2}=4,$ and ${\sigma }_{3}=0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
feedback.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={6}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={6}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=6.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=6.$

Question 10
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=7, σ2=23, and σ3=0, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
14
b
7
c
43
d
7
e
23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=7, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=72. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=72⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=7.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=7.

feedback.problem: A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=7,$ ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{3},$ and ${\sigma }_{3}=0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
feedback.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=7,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={7}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={7}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=7.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=7.$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/6be1f51600ae7b42ad0c4c8f67eb8f3ba3570606ec4e3e5e75c65df397aab060.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=7={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=5={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=7$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Problems Regarding the Image of the Unit Eigenvectors of a Quadratic Form
last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=7={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=5={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=7$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

question.html:
Question 11
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
7 and 5
b
v1 and v1
c
7 and 5
d
7 and 10
e
7v1 and 5v1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=7=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=5=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=7 and σ2=5.

solution.reasoning: For a unit eigenvector v_i of A^T A with eigenvalue \lambda_i, \|Av_i\|=\sqrt{\lambda_i}=\sigma_i. The current diagram labels these principal semi-axis lengths as 7 and 5, so the nonzero singular values are 7 and 5, choice c. No Math Academy answer evidence for this current question is supplied.

Question 11
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
7 and 5
b
v1 and v1
c
7 and 5
d
7 and 10
e
7v1 and 5v1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=7=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=5=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=7 and σ2=5.

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/f9b7a55ee1b8d3327ae9da740feaafde459daaee4e42a27cf26fd0ac8e63f20b.png)

A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $36$ of ${A}^{T}A?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=6={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={6}^{2}=36,$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=2={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={2}^{2}=4.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=36$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{1}.$

question.html:
Question 12
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue 36 of ATA?

a
2
b
6
c
v2
d
6v1+2v2
e
v1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=6=σ1, which means that λ1=62=36, and

  • ||Av2||=2=σ2, which means that λ2=22=4.

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ1=36 of ATA is v1.
question.knowledge_point: Solving Problems Regarding the Image of the Unit Eigenvectors of a Quadratic Form

solution.reasoning: For a unit eigenvector v_i, its eigenvalue is \|Av_i\|^2. The current diagram gives \|Av_1\|=6 and \|Av_2\|=2, so v_1 corresponds to 36 and v_2 to 4. Choose e. The worked example uses a different diagram and does not establish Math Academy's current answer key.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/f9b7a55ee1b8d3327ae9da740feaafde459daaee4e42a27cf26fd0ac8e63f20b.png)

A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $36$ of ${A}^{T}A?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=6={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={6}^{2}=36,$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=2={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={2}^{2}=4.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=36$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{1}.$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Problems Regarding the Image of the Unit Eigenvectors of a Quadratic Form
last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=10={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={10}^{2}=100,$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=8={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={8}^{2}=64.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=100$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{1}.$

Question 13
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue 100 of ATA?

a
AATv1
b
Av1
c
v2
d
v1
e
Av2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=10=σ1, which means that λ1=102=100, and

  • ||Av2||=8=σ2, which means that λ2=82=64.

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ1=100 of ATA is v1.

solution.reasoning: For a unit eigenvector v_i of A^T A, its eigenvalue equals \|Av_i\|^2. The current diagram shows \|Av_1\|=10, so A^T A v_1=100v_1. Thus choice d is correct; v_2 instead corresponds to 8^2=64. The supplied example does not capture Math Academy's answer key for this question.

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=5={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=3={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

question.html:
Question 14
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
6 and 4
b
7 and 3
c
5 and 3
d
11 and 7
e
25 and 9
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=5=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=3=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=5 and σ2=3.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=5={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=3={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
6 and 4
b
7 and 3
c
5 and 3
d
11 and 7
e
25 and 9
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=5=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=3=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=5 and σ2=3.
