question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/57368434b3025dc777c5be725da43e365dfd8ef3c47049570c0ecb13f2baf035.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=9={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=4={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14175654/assets/57368434b3025dc777c5be725da43e365dfd8ef3c47049570c0ecb13f2baf035.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=9={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=4={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$

Question 15
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that v1 and v2 are unit eigenvectors of ATA, what are the nonzero singular values of A?

a
9 and 4
b
18 and 8
c
3 and 2
d
v1 and v1
e
9v1 and 4v1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose A is an m×n matrix. Let

{v1,v2…,vn} be an orthonormal basis of Rn consisting of the eigenvectors of ATA with corresponding eigenvalues

λ1≥λ2≥…≥λn.

Then,

  • σ1=λ1 is the length of Av1,

  • σ2=λ2 is the length of Av2,

  • ⋯

In our example, we see that

  • ||Av1||=9=σ1, and

  • ||Av2||=4=σ2.

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of A are σ1=9 and σ2=4.

solution.reasoning: For each unit eigenvector v_i of A^T A, the corresponding singular value is \sigma_i=\|Av_i\|. The current diagram labels these lengths as 9 and 4, so choice a is correct. The supplied example supports this rule but does not capture Math Academy's answer key for the current question.

questions.problem: Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB}$, $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$, given the points $A(1,2,-1)$, $B(2,3,1)$, $C(4,1,2)$, and $D(1,4,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(2i+3j+k)-(i+2j-k) \\  & =i+j+2k \\  & =⟨1,1,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(4i+j+2k)-(i+2j-k) \\  & =3i-j+3k \\  & =⟨3,-1,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(i+4j+2k)-(i+2j-k) \\  & =2j+3k \\  & =⟨0,2,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =((-1)\cdot 3-2\cdot 3)-(3\cdot 3-0\cdot 3)+2(3\cdot 2-0\cdot (-1)) \\  & =-9-9+12 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelpiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|-6|=6.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors $a=⟨-1,1,1⟩$, $b=⟨2,1,0⟩$, and $c=⟨k,-2,-3⟩$ are coplanar.
questions.worked_solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ k & -2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ k & -3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ k & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(1\cdot (-3)-(-2)\cdot 0)-(2\cdot (-3)-k\cdot 0)+(2\cdot (-2)-k\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6-4-k \\  & =5-k.\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 5-k & =0 \\ k & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=5.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $\overset{\to }{AD},$ given the points $A(7,6,4),$ $B(8,5,9),$ $C(7,4,2),$ and $D(5,7,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(8i+5j+9k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =i-j+5k \\  & =⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(7i+4j+2k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =-2j-2k \\  & =⟨0,-2,-2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(5i+7j+4k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =-2i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}|+5\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =((-2)\cdot 0-1\cdot (-2))+(0\cdot 0-(-2)\cdot (-2))+5(0\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-2)) \\  & =2-4-20 \\  & =-22.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|-22|=22.
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Find $k$ given that the vectors $x=⟨1,k,2⟩$, $y=⟨5,-2,3⟩$, and $z=⟨-4,k,1⟩$ are coplanar.

$k=${{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (y\times z) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & k & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & 3 \\ -4 & k & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ k & 1\end{aligned}|-k\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -4 & k\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-2\cdot 1-3\cdot k)-k(5\cdot 1-3\cdot -4)+2(5k-(-2)(-4)) \\  & =-2-3k-k(5+12)+2(5k-8) \\  & =-2-3k-17k+10k-16 \\  & =-10k-18\end{aligned}
$$

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (y\times z) & =0 \\ -10k-18 & =0 \\ k & =-\frac{9}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\frac{9}{5}.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Calculate the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD},$ given the points $A(-1,0,1),$ $B(2,-3,4),$ $C(-2,-2,2),$ and $D(0,-1,5).$

$V=${{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(2i-3j+4k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =3i-3j+3k \\  & =⟨3,-3,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(-2i-2j+2k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =-i-2j+1k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(-j+5k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =i-j+4k \\  & =⟨1,-1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 3 \\ -1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}|-(-3)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(-8+1)+3(-4-1)+3(1-(-2)) \\  & =-21-15+9 \\  & =-27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|-27|=27.
$$

question.worked_solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(2i+3j+k)-(i+2j-k) \\  & =i+j+2k \\  & =⟨1,1,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(4i+j+2k)-(i+2j-k) \\  & =3i-j+3k \\  & =⟨3,-1,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(i+4j+2k)-(i+2j-k) \\  & =2j+3k \\  & =⟨0,2,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =((-1)\cdot 3-2\cdot 3)-(3\cdot 3-0\cdot 3)+2(3\cdot 2-0\cdot (-1)) \\  & =-9-9+12 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}

$$

AB→=b−a=(2i+3j+k)−(i+2j−k)=i+j+2k=⟨1,1,2⟩AC→=c−a=(4i+j+2k)−(i+2j−k)=3i−j+3k=⟨3,−1,3⟩AD→=d−a=(i+4j+2k)−(i+2j−k)=2j+3k=⟨0,2,3⟩

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

AB→⋅(AC→×AD→)=|1123−13023|=1⋅|−1323|−1⋅|3303|+2⋅|3−102|=((−1)⋅3−2⋅3)−(3⋅3−0⋅3)+2(3⋅2−0⋅(−1))=−9−9+12=−6.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors $a=⟨-1,1,1⟩$, $b=⟨2,1,0⟩$, and $c=⟨k,-2,-3⟩$ are coplanar.
question.worked_solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ k & -2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ k & -3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ k & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(1\cdot (-3)-(-2)\cdot 0)-(2\cdot (-3)-k\cdot 0)+(2\cdot (-2)-k\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6-4-k \\  & =5-k.\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 5-k & =0 \\ k & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=5.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $\overset{\to }{AD},$ given the points $A(7,6,4),$ $B(8,5,9),$ $C(7,4,2),$ and $D(5,7,4).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(8i+5j+9k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =i-j+5k \\  & =⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(7i+4j+2k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =-2j-2k \\  & =⟨0,-2,-2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(5i+7j+4k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =-2i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}|+5\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =((-2)\cdot 0-1\cdot (-2))+(0\cdot 0-(-2)\cdot (-2))+5(0\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-2)) \\  & =2-4-20 \\  & =-22.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|-22|=22.
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we find the displacement vectors AB→, AC→, and AD→ that span the parallelepiped:

AB→=b−a=(8i+5j+9k)−(7i+6j+4k)=i−j+5k=⟨1,−1,5⟩AC→=c−a=(7i+4j+2k)−(7i+6j+4k)=−2j−2k=⟨0,−2,−2⟩AD→=d−a=(5i+7j+4k)−(7i+6j+4k)=−2i+j=⟨−2,1,0⟩

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

AB→⋅(AC→×AD→)=|1−150−2−2−210|=1⋅|−2−210|−(−1)⋅|0−2−20|+5⋅|0−2−21|=((−2)⋅0−1⋅(−2))+(0⋅0−(−2)⋅(−2))+5(0⋅1−(−2)⋅(−2))=2−4−20=−22.

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by AB→, AC→, and AD→ is

V=|−22|=22.

question.problem:
Find $k$ given that the vectors $x=⟨1,k,2⟩$, $y=⟨5,-2,3⟩$, and $z=⟨-4,k,1⟩$ are coplanar.

$k=${{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (y\times z) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & k & 2 \\ 5 & -2 & 3 \\ -4 & k & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ k & 1\end{aligned}|-k\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -4 & k\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-2\cdot 1-3\cdot k)-k(5\cdot 1-3\cdot -4)+2(5k-(-2)(-4)) \\  & =-2-3k-k(5+12)+2(5k-8) \\  & =-2-3k-17k+10k-16 \\  & =-10k-18\end{aligned}
$$

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (y\times z) & =0 \\ -10k-18 & =0 \\ k & =-\frac{9}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\frac{9}{5}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Calculate the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD},$ given the points $A(-1,0,1),$ $B(2,-3,4),$ $C(-2,-2,2),$ and $D(0,-1,5).$

$V=${{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(2i-3j+4k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =3i-3j+3k \\  & =⟨3,-3,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(-2i-2j+2k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =-i-2j+1k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(-j+5k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =i-j+4k \\  & =⟨1,-1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 3 \\ -1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}|-(-3)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(-8+1)+3(-4-1)+3(1-(-2)) \\  & =-21-15+9 \\  & =-27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|-27|=27.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14176224/assets/aec20235a2968f30f1ac3861d429a4102464a701fff0a90c13dae97334735273.png)

Consider the diagram above. Which of the following statements is true?

I. $∠A$ is null

II. $∠B$ is acute

III. $∠C$ is obtuse
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. From the diagram, it follows that $m∠A={180}^{∘}>{0}^{∘}.$

- Statement II is true, and statement III is false. Indeed, from the graph we deduce  that 

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠B+{100}^{∘}+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+m∠C & ={80}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the measure of each of the angles $∠B$ and $∠C$ is less than ${80}^{∘},$ so these angles are acute angles.

So, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Let $∠S$ and $∠T$ be two adjacent angles. Given that $∠S$ is a straight angle and $∠T$ is obtuse, what type of angle is their sum?
questions.worked_solution:
Since $∠S$ is a straight angle, we have 

$$
m∠S={180}^{∘}.
$$

 Since $∠T$ is obtuse, we have

$$
{90}^{∘}<m∠T<{180}^{∘}.
$$

So, the sum of these two angles satisfies by the following inequalies:

$$
\begin{aligned}{180}^{∘}+{90}^{∘} & <m∠S+m∠T<{180}^{∘}+{180}^{∘} \\ {270}^{∘} & <m∠S+m∠T<{360}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sum of $∠S$ and $∠T$ is a reflex angle.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Let $∠N$ and $∠S$ be two adjacent angles. Given that $∠N$ is a null angle and $∠S$ is straight, what type of angle is their sum?
questions.worked_solution:
Since $∠N$ is a null and a right angle, we have

$$
m∠N={0}^{∘}
$$

and since $∠S$ is a straight angle, we have

$$
m∠S={180}^{∘}.
$$

So, their sum is 

$$
m∠N+m∠S={0}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}={180}^{∘}.
$$

Consequently, the sum of $∠N$ and $∠S$ is a straight angle.

In the figure shown above, determine the measure of $∠GOH$ given that $m∠BOD={120}^{∘}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagram, $∠AOC$ and $∠EOG$ are vertical angles. Since vertical angles are congruent, we have

$$
m∠AOC=m∠EOG={90}^{∘}.
$$

On the other hand, since $∠AOC$ is a right angle, the angle addition postulate gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AOB+m∠BOC & =m∠AOC \\ {30}^{∘}+m∠BOC & ={90}^{∘} \\ m∠BOC & ={60}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, given that $m∠BOD={120}^{∘}$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠BOC+m∠COD & =m∠BOD \\ {60}^{∘}+m∠COD & ={120}^{∘} \\ m∠COD & ={60}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $∠COD$ and $∠GOH$ are vertical angles. Therefore, 

$$
m∠GOH=m∠COD={60}^{∘}.
$$

Consider the diagram above. Which of the following statements is true?

I. $\angle A$ is obtuse

II. $\angle B$ is a right angle

III. $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ are vertical angles
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. From the diagram, $\angle A$ and the angle with measure $130^\circ$ are vertical angles. Therefore, 

$$
m\angle A = 130^\circ >    90^\circ.
$$

Consequently, $\angle A$ is an obtuse angle.

- Statement II is false. From the diagram, $\angle B$ and the angle with measure $50^\circ$ are vertical angles. Therefore, 

$$
m\angle B = 50^\circ \neq    90^\circ.
$$

Consequently, $\angle B$ is not a right angle.

- Statement III is false. Angles $\angle A$ and $\angle B$  are not vertical since they have a common side.

So, the correct answer is "I only."

                    Identifying an Angle Type From a Description
canonical_examples.problem: Let $\angle S$ and $\angle T$ be two adjacent angles. Given that $\angle S$ is a straight angle and $\angle T$ is right, what type of angle is their sum?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $\angle S$ is a straight angle, we have

$$
m\angle S=180^\circ,
$$

and since $\angle T$ is a right angle, we have 

$$
m\angle T=90^{\circ}.
$$

So, their sum is 

$$
m\angle S + m\angle T=180^{\circ} + 90^{\circ}=270^{\circ}.
$$

Consequently, the sum of $\angle S$ and $\angle T$ is a reflex angle.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When solving problems with angles, it is helpful to remember the following classifications:

- a **null** angle has a measure of $0^\circ,$

- an **acute** angle has a measure between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ,$

- a **right** angle has a measure of $90^\circ,$

- an **obtuse** angle has a measure between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ,$

- a **straight** angle has a measure of $180^\circ,$

- a **reflex** angle has a measure between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ,$ and

- a **full** angle has a measure of $360^\circ.$

It is also helpful to remember that when two lines meet at a point, the opposite angles are called **vertical angles**. Vertical angles are congruent, and consequently they have the same measure.

It is also helpful to remember that when two lines meet at a point, the opposite angles are called **vertical angles**. Vertical angles are congruent, and consequently they have the same measure.
tutorial.content:
When solving problems with angles, it is helpful to remember the following classifications:

- a **null** angle has a measure of $0^\circ,$

- an **acute** angle has a measure between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ,$

- a **right** angle has a measure of $90^\circ,$

- an **obtuse** angle has a measure between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ,$

- a **straight** angle has a measure of $180^\circ,$

- a **reflex** angle has a measure between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ,$ and

- a **full** angle has a measure of $360^\circ.$

It is also helpful to remember that when two lines meet at a point, the opposite angles are called **vertical angles**. Vertical angles are congruent, and consequently they have the same measure.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Let $∠S$ and $∠T$ be two adjacent angles. Given that $∠S$ is a straight angle and $∠T$ is obtuse, what type of angle is their sum?
question.worked_solution:
Since $∠S$ is a straight angle, we have 

$$
m∠S={180}^{∘}.
$$

 Since $∠T$ is obtuse, we have

$$
{90}^{∘}<m∠T<{180}^{∘}.
$$

So, the sum of these two angles satisfies by the following inequalies:

$$
\begin{aligned}{180}^{∘}+{90}^{∘} & <m∠S+m∠T<{180}^{∘}+{180}^{∘} \\ {270}^{∘} & <m∠S+m∠T<{360}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sum of $∠S$ and $∠T$ is a reflex angle.

In the figure shown above, determine the measure of $∠GOH$ given that $m∠BOD={120}^{∘}.$
question.worked_solution:
From the diagram, $∠AOC$ and $∠EOG$ are vertical angles. Since vertical angles are congruent, we have

$$
m∠AOC=m∠EOG={90}^{∘}.
$$

On the other hand, since $∠AOC$ is a right angle, the angle addition postulate gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AOB+m∠BOC & =m∠AOC \\ {30}^{∘}+m∠BOC & ={90}^{∘} \\ m∠BOC & ={60}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, given that $m∠BOD={120}^{∘}$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠BOC+m∠COD & =m∠BOD \\ {60}^{∘}+m∠COD & ={120}^{∘} \\ m∠COD & ={60}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $∠COD$ and $∠GOH$ are vertical angles. Therefore, 

$$
m∠GOH=m∠COD={60}^{∘}.
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
From the diagram, $∠AOC$ and $∠EOG$ are vertical angles. Since vertical angles are congruent, we have

$$
m∠AOC=m∠EOG={90}^{∘}.
$$

On the other hand, since $∠AOC$ is a right angle, the angle addition postulate gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AOB+m∠BOC & =m∠AOC \\ {30}^{∘}+m∠BOC & ={90}^{∘} \\ m∠BOC & ={60}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, given that $m∠BOD={120}^{∘}$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠BOC+m∠COD & =m∠BOD \\ {60}^{∘}+m∠COD & ={120}^{∘} \\ m∠COD & ={60}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $∠COD$ and $∠GOH$ are vertical angles. Therefore, 

$$
m∠GOH=m∠COD={60}^{∘}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14168954/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{a\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 3+3\cdot 7+(-3)(-6)+1\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{6+21+18+1}{4+9+9+1}a \\  & =\frac{46}{23}a \\  & =2a \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}\{a\}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}\{a\},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Find the distance between $x$ and $\text{Span}\{b\}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The distance between the vector $x$ and the vector space $\text{Span}\{b\}$ is given by $‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖$, where $\overset{^}{x}$ in the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{span}\{b\}.$

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{b\cdot x}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 2+1\cdot (-2)+(-1)(-2)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-2-2-2+2}{1+1+1+1}b \\  & =-b \\  & =-1[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{((-2)-(-1))^{2}+(2-1)^{2}+((-2)-(-1))^{2}+((-2)-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1+9} \\  & =\sqrt{12} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance  Between a Vector and a One-Dimensional Subspace
questions.raw_html:
2.Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a One-Dimensional Subspace?

Let x=[−22−2−2] and b=[1−11−1]. Find the distance between x and Span{b}.

E
Tue, Oct 13th @ 9:15 AM|Elapsed: 0:21Correct

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{11\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-8}{2}b \\  & =-4b \\  & =-4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=6{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 6+5\cdot 2+0\cdot 1}{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{82}{41}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -5 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=5{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-9)\cdot 5+(-5)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 1}{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60\,}{\,\,\,30\,}b \\  & =-2b \\  & =-2[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto the Solution Space of a System of Equations
questions.raw_html:
5.Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto the Solution Space of a System of Equations?

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[−9−5−5],{x1−3x2+x3=0x1−2x2−x3=0

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14168954/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{a\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 3+3\cdot 7+(-3)(-6)+1\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{6+21+18+1}{4+9+9+1}a \\  & =\frac{46}{23}a \\  & =2a \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}\{a\}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}\{a\},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

Let x=[37−61] and a=[23−31]. If x=y+z, where y∈Span{a} and z⊥Span{a}, then z=

b

projax=a⋅xa⋅aa=2⋅3+3⋅7+(−3)(−6)+1⋅122+32+(−3)2+12a=6+21+18+14+9+9+1a=4623a=2a=2[23−31]=[46−62].

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The distance between the vector $x$ and the vector space $\text{Span}\{b\}$ is given by $‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖$, where $\overset{^}{x}$ in the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{span}\{b\}.$

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{b\cdot x}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 2+1\cdot (-2)+(-1)(-2)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-2-2-2+2}{1+1+1+1}b \\  & =-b \\  & =-1[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{((-2)-(-1))^{2}+(2-1)^{2}+((-2)-(-1))^{2}+((-2)-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1+9} \\  & =\sqrt{12} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Let x=[−22−2−2] and b=[1−11−1]. Find the distance between x and Span{b}.

a
23
b
3
c
32
d
22
e
33
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The distance between the vector x and the vector space Span{b} is given by ‖x−x^‖, where x^ in the orthogonal projection of x onto span{b}.

First, we find the orthogonal projection of x onto Span{b}. projbx=b⋅xb⋅bb=1⋅(−2)+(−1)⋅2+1⋅(−2)+(−1)(−2)(1)2+(−1)2+(1)2+(−1)2b=−2−2−2+21+1+1+1b=−b=−1[1−11−1]=[−11−11]=x^.

Therefore, ‖x−x^‖=(x1−x^1)2+(x2−x^2)2+(x3−x^3)2+(x4−x^4)2=((−2)−(−1))2+(2−1)2+((−2)−(−1))2+((−2)−1)2=1+1+1+9=12=23.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{11\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-8}{2}b \\  & =-4b \\  & =-4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

b

EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[110220]R2:=R2−2R1∼[110000].

In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we get x1=−x2. So, the general solution is [−x2x2]=x2[−11],x2∈R.

Consequently, B={[−11]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system: projbx=x⋅bb⋅bb=11⋅(−1)+3⋅1(−1)2+12b=−82b=−4b=−4[−11]=[4−4]

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=6{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 6+5\cdot 2+0\cdot 1}{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{82}{41}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:

x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=5{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-9)\cdot 5+(-5)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 1}{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60\,}{\,\,\,30\,}b \\  & =-2b \\  & =-2[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[−9−5−5],{x1−3x2+x3=0x1−2x2−x3=0

a
[104−2]
b
[521]
c
[−10−4−2]
d
[−5−2−1]
e
[5−4−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[1−3101−2−10]R2:=R2−R1∼[1−31001−20]

In the reduced matrix above, there are 2 pivot columns (1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get x2=2x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

x1−3⋅(2x3)+x3=0⟹x1=5x3.

So, the general solution is [5x32x3x3]=x3[521],x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[521]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system:

projbx=x⋅bb⋅bb=(−9)⋅5+(−5)⋅2+(−5)⋅152+22+12b=−6030b=−2b=−2[521]=[−10−4−2]

The projection coefficient is (x·b)/(b·b)=-4/4=-1, so the perpendicular residual is x+b=(-1,1,-1,-3). Its norm is sqrt(12)=2\sqrt{3}, option a. This agrees with my earlier answer, the submitted value graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

The solution space is Span{(1,-1)}. Projecting (11,3) gives ((11-3)/2)(1,-1)=(4,-4), option a, with orthogonal residual (7,7). The actual submission was option b, (-4,-4), which fails x₁+x₂=0, so its Incorrect grade is consistent.

The equations give x₂=2x₃ and x₁=6x₃, so the solution space is Span{(6,2,1)}. The projection coefficient is (72+10)/41=2, yielding (12,4,2), option e. The residual (0,1,-2) is orthogonal to (6,2,1). My earlier answer matches both the submitted value graded Correct and Math Academy's worked solution.

question.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ If $x=y+z,$ where $y\in \text{Span}\{a\}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}\{a\},$ then $z=$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14168954/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{a\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 3+3\cdot 7+(-3)(-6)+1\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{6+21+18+1}{4+9+9+1}a \\  & =\frac{46}{23}a \\  & =2a \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}\{a\}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}\{a\},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

Let x=[37−61] and a=[23−31]. If x=y+z, where y∈Span{a} and z⊥Span{a}, then z=

a
z=[110−1]
b
z=[101−1]
c
z=[−1101]
d
z=[−110−1]
e
z=[−101−1]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the orthogonal projection of x onto Span{a}:

projax=a⋅xa⋅aa=2⋅3+3⋅7+(−3)(−6)+1⋅122+32+(−3)2+12a=6+21+18+14+9+9+1a=4623a=2a=2[23−31]=[46−62].

Therefore, we get the following:

y=projax=[46−62]z=x−projax=[37−61]−[46−62]=[−110−1]

Notice that y∈Span{a} and z⊥Span{a}, as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, z=[−110−1].

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14168954/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{a\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 3+3\cdot 7+(-3)(-6)+1\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{6+21+18+1}{4+9+9+1}a \\  & =\frac{46}{23}a \\  & =2a \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 7 \\ -6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}\{a\}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}\{a\},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Find the distance between $x$ and $\text{Span}\{b\}.$
question.worked_solution:
The distance between the vector $x$ and the vector space $\text{Span}\{b\}$ is given by $‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖$, where $\overset{^}{x}$ in the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{span}\{b\}.$

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{b\}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{b\cdot x}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 2+1\cdot (-2)+(-1)(-2)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-2-2-2+2}{1+1+1+1}b \\  & =-b \\  & =-1[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{((-2)-(-1))^{2}+(2-1)^{2}+((-2)-(-1))^{2}+((-2)-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1+9} \\  & =\sqrt{12} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{11\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-8}{2}b \\  & =-4b \\  & =-4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[110220]R2:=R2−2R1∼[110000].

Consequently, B={[−11]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{11\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-8}{2}b \\  & =-4b \\  & =-4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[110220]R2:=R2−2R1∼[110000].

In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we get x1=−x2. So, the general solution is [−x2x2]=x2[−11],x2∈R.

Consequently, B={[−11]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system: projbx=x⋅bb⋅bb=11⋅(−1)+3⋅1(−1)2+12b=−82b=−4b=−4[−11]=[4−4]

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{11\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-8}{2}b \\  & =-4b \\  & =-4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=6{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 6+5\cdot 2+0\cdot 1}{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{82}{41}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[1250],{x1−3x2=03x1−5x2−8x3=0

a
[1205]
b
[−1205]
c
[640]
d
[1250]
e
[1242]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[1−3003−5−80]R2:=R2−3R1∼[1−30004−80]

In the reduced matrix above, there are 2 pivot columns (1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get x2=2x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

x1−3⋅(2x3)=0⟹x1=6x3.

So, the general solution is [6x32x3x3]=x3[621],x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[621]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system:

projbx=x⋅bb⋅bb=12⋅6+5⋅2+0⋅162+22+12b=8241b=2b=2[621]=[1242]

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=6{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 6+5\cdot 2+0\cdot 1}{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{82}{41}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

feedback.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=6{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 6+5\cdot 2+0\cdot 1}{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{82}{41}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -5 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=5{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-9)\cdot 5+(-5)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 1}{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60\,}{\,\,\,30\,}b \\  & =-2b \\  & =-2[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[−9−5−5],{x1−3x2+x3=0x1−2x2−x3=0

a
[104−2]
b
[521]
c
[−10−4−2]
d
[−5−2−1]
e
[5−4−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[1−3101−2−10]R2:=R2−R1∼[1−31001−20]

In the reduced matrix above, there are 2 pivot columns (1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get x2=2x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

x1−3⋅(2x3)+x3=0⟹x1=5x3.

So, the general solution is [5x32x3x3]=x3[521],x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[521]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system:

projbx=x⋅bb⋅bb=(−9)⋅5+(−5)⋅2+(−5)⋅152+22+12b=−6030b=−2b=−2[521]=[−10−4−2]

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=5{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-9)\cdot 5+(-5)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 1}{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60\,}{\,\,\,30\,}b \\  & =-2b \\  & =-2[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -5 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[−9−5−5],{x1−3x2+x3=0x1−2x2−x3=0

a
[104−2]
b
[521]
c
[−10−4−2]
d
[−5−2−1]
e
[5−4−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[1−3101−2−10]R2:=R2−R1∼[1−31001−20]

In the reduced matrix above, there are 2 pivot columns (1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get x2=2x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

x1−3⋅(2x3)+x3=0⟹x1=5x3.

So, the general solution is [5x32x3x3]=x3[521],x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[521]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system:

projbx=x⋅bb⋅bb=(−9)⋅5+(−5)⋅2+(−5)⋅152+22+12b=−6030b=−2b=−2[521]=[−10−4−2]

solution.reasoning: Subtracting the second equation from the first gives x₂=2x₃, and substitution gives x₁=5x₃. Thus the solution space is Span{(5,2,1)}. The projection coefficient is (-9·5-5·2-5·1)/(25+4+1)=-60/30=-2, giving (-10,-4,-2), option c. The residual (1,-1,-3) is orthogonal to (5,2,1). feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -5 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=5{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-9)\cdot 5+(-5)\cdot 2+(-5)\cdot 1}{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60\,}{\,\,\,30\,}b \\  & =-2b \\  & =-2[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

a
[104−2]
b
[521]
c
[−10−4−2]
d
[−5−2−1]
e
[5−4−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[1−3101−2−10]R2:=R2−R1∼[1−31001−20]

In the reduced matrix above, there are 2 pivot columns (1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get x2=2x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

x1−3⋅(2x3)+x3=0⟹x1=5x3.

So, the general solution is [5x32x3x3]=x3[521],x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[521]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system:

projbx=x⋅bb⋅bb=(−9)⋅5+(−5)⋅2+(−5)⋅152+22+12b=−6030b=−2b=−2[521]=[−10−4−2]

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
Since $5.8$ is larger than $3,$ the answer will be negative.

We start by solving an easier problem, which is to carry out the subtraction in the reverse order:

$$
5.8-3=2.8
$$

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
3-5.8=-2.8
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

Since 8.7 is larger than 6, the answer will be negative.

We start by solving an easier problem, which is to carry out the subtraction in the reverse order:

8.7−6=2.7

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above.

Therefore, we conclude that

6−8.7=−2.7

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true? 

I. The sum of $4{x}^{2}+1$ and $2{x}^{2}$ is a binomial.

II. The sum of $3{x}^{2}-2x$ and $5$ is a binomial.

III. The sum of a binomial and a monomial is **sometimes** a binomial.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
(4{x}^{2}+1)+(2{x}^{2})=6{x}^{2}+1,
$$

which is a binomial.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
(3{x}^{2}-2x)+(5)=3{x}^{2}-2x+5,
$$

which is *not* a binomial (it's a trinomial).

- Statement III is true. The sum of a binomial and a monomial *could be* a binomial (see, for example, statement I). 

 However, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *not always* a binomial (see, for example, statement II). 

 So, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *sometimes* binomial.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

question.worked_solution:
The polynomial ${z}^{5}-3z$ has two terms, so it is a binomial.

Also, its degree is $5,$ so it is a quintic.

Therefore, the polynomial is a quintic binomial.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Which of the following statements are true? 

I. The sum of $4{x}^{2}+1$ and $2{x}^{2}$ is a binomial.

II. The sum of $3{x}^{2}-2x$ and $5$ is a binomial.

III. The sum of a binomial and a monomial is **sometimes** a binomial.
question.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
(4{x}^{2}+1)+(2{x}^{2})=6{x}^{2}+1,
$$

which is a binomial.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
(3{x}^{2}-2x)+(5)=3{x}^{2}-2x+5,
$$

which is *not* a binomial (it's a trinomial).

- Statement III is true. The sum of a binomial and a monomial *could be* a binomial (see, for example, statement I). 

 However, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *not always* a binomial (see, for example, statement II). 

 So, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *sometimes* binomial.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

choices.html: II only
II and III only
I and III only
I only
I, II, and III

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{1\cdot (-1)+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{1\cdot 3+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{1\cdot 0+4\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(21[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{0\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
3.Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors?

Consider the vector x and the subspace S=Span{a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[−102−2],a2=[2021],a3=[20−1−2],x=[0−1−3−12]. Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S given that the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6 \\ 14\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{10\cdot (-2)+6\cdot 1+14\cdot 3}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{10\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}w=3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+4\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{7\cdot (-3)+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-1)[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors
questions.raw_html:
5.Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors?

Consider the vector x and the subspace S=Span{a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[1−110],a2=[1102],a3=[−3−122],x=[73−14].

Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S given that the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal.

M
Tue, Oct 13th @ 9:22 AM|Elapsed: 0:18Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$

$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
