Question 1
?

Consider the vector x and the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[−111],w=[211],x=[314]. Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the plane given that v⊥w.

a
[25454]
b
[352]
c
[32525]
d
[35252]
e
[52352]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. And, since the set {v,w} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=projvx+projwx.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1} and Span{a2}:

projvx=x⋅vv⋅vv=3⋅(−1)+1⋅1+4⋅1(−1)2+12+12v=23[−111]projwx=x⋅ww⋅ww=3⋅2+1⋅1+4⋅122+12+12w=116[211]

Therefore, we have that projSx=projvx+projwx=23[−111]+116[211]=16(4[−111]+11[211])=[35252].

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{1\cdot (-1)+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{1\cdot 3+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{1\cdot 0+4\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(21[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
question.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{1\cdot (-1)+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{1\cdot 3+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{1\cdot 0+4\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(21[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{10\cdot (-2)+6\cdot 1+14\cdot 3}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{10\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}w=3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{10\cdot (-2)+6\cdot 1+14\cdot 3}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{10\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}w=3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the vector x and the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[−213],w=[2−22],x=[10614]. Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the plane given that v⊥w.

a
 [21012]
b
 [8102]
c
 [24−6]
d
 [8−42]
e
[2−412]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. And, since the set {v,w} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=projvx+projwx.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1} and Span{a2}:

projvx=x⋅vv⋅vv=10⋅(−2)+6⋅1+14⋅3(−2)2+12+32v=2[−213]=[−426]projwx=x⋅ww⋅ww=10⋅2+6⋅(−2)+14⋅222+(−2)2+22w=3[2−22]=[6−66]

Therefore, we have that projSx=projvx+projwx=[−426]+[6−66]=[2−412].

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+4\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{7\cdot (-3)+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-1)[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
question.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+4\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{7\cdot (-3)+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-1)[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Consider the vector x and the subspace S=Span{a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[1−110],a2=[1102],a3=[−3−122],x=[73−14].

Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S given that the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal.

a
 [−3−122]
b
[−3−122]
c
[−1102]
d
 [−1−132]
e
[73−14]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1}, Span{a2}, and Span{a3}:

proja1x=x⋅a1a1⋅a1a1=7⋅1+3⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅1+4⋅012+(−1)2+12+02a1=[1−110]proja2x=x⋅a2a2⋅a2a2=7⋅1+3⋅1+(−1)⋅0+4⋅212+12+02+22a2=3[1102]proja3x=x⋅a3a3⋅a3a3=7⋅(−3)+3⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅2+4⋅2(−3)2+(−1)2+22+22a2=−[−3−122]

Therefore, we have that

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x=[1−110]+3[1102]+(−1)[−3−122]=[1−110]+[3306]+[31−2−2]=[73−14].

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
question.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Consider the vector x and the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[−111],w=[211],x=[314]. Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the plane given that v⊥w.

a
[25454]
b
[352]
c
[32525]
d
[35252]
e
[52352]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. And, since the set {v,w} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=projvx+projwx.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1} and Span{a2}:

projvx=x⋅vv⋅vv=3⋅(−1)+1⋅1+4⋅1(−1)2+12+12v=23[−111]projwx=x⋅ww⋅ww=3⋅2+1⋅1+4⋅122+12+12w=116[211]

Therefore, we have that projSx=projvx+projwx=23[−111]+116[211]=16(4[−111]+11[211])=[35252].

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$

EXPLANATION

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. And, since the set {v,w} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=projvx+projwx.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1} and Span{a2}:

projvx=x⋅vv⋅vv=3⋅(−1)+1⋅1+4⋅1(−1)2+12+12v=23[−111]projwx=x⋅ww⋅ww=3⋅2+1⋅1+4⋅122+12+12w=116[211]

Therefore, we have that projSx=projvx+projwx=23[−111]+116[211]=16(4[−111]+11[211])=[35252].

solution.reasoning: The vectors are orthogonal because v·w=-2+1+1=0. Thus the projection is ((x·v)/(v·v))v+((x·w)/(w·w))w=(2/3)v+(11/6)w=[3,5/2,5/2], which is option d. Mathematical correctness is established, but no Math Academy answer or grade was captured.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
question.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{1\cdot (-1)+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{1\cdot 3+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{1\cdot 0+4\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(21[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{1\cdot (-1)+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{1\cdot 3+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{1\cdot 0+4\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(21[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

Since the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1}, Span{a2}, and Span{a3}:

proja1x=x⋅a1a1⋅a1a1=1⋅(−1)+4⋅1+3⋅1+1⋅1(−1)2+12+12+12a1=74[−1111]proja2x=x⋅a2a2⋅a2a2=1⋅3+4⋅1+3⋅1+1⋅132+12+12+12a2=1112[3111]proja3x=x⋅a3a3⋅a3a3=1⋅0+4⋅(−2)+3⋅1+1⋅102+(−2)2+12+12a2=−23[0−211]

Therefore, we have that projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x=74[−1111]+1112[3111]−23[0−211]=112(21[−1111]+11[3111]−8[0−211])=[1422].

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
feedback.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{1\cdot (-1)+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{1\cdot 3+4\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{1\cdot 0+4\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{11}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(21[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+11[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
question.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{0\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{0\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
question.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{0\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the vector x and the subspace S=Span{a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[−102−2],a2=[2021],a3=[20−1−2],x=[0−1−3−12]. Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S given that the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal.

a
[0−10−12]
b
[303−3]
c
[11−30]
d
[00−3−12]
e
[10−1−12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1}, Span{a2}, and Span{a3}:

proja1x=x⋅a1a1⋅a1a1=0⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅0+(−3)⋅2+(−12)⋅(−2)(−1)2+02+22+(−2)2a1=[−204−4]proja2x=x⋅a2a2⋅a2a2=0⋅2+(−1)⋅0+(−3)⋅2+(−12)⋅122+02+22+12a2=[−40−4−2]proja3x=x⋅a3a3⋅a3a3=0⋅2+(−1)⋅0+(−3)⋅(−1)+(−12)⋅(−2)22+02+(−1)2+(−2)2a2=[60−3−6]

Therefore, we have that

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x=[−204−4]+[−40−4−2]+[60−3−6]=[00−3−12].

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
feedback.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{0\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot 2+(-12)\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-12)\cdot (-2)}{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6 \\ 14\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
question.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{10\cdot (-2)+6\cdot 1+14\cdot 3}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{10\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}w=3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4

Consider the vector x and the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[−213],w=[2−22],x=[10614]. Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the plane given that v⊥w.

a
 [21012]
b
 [8102]
c
 [24−6]
d
 [8−42]
e
[2−412]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. And, since the set {v,w} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=projvx+projwx.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1} and Span{a2}:

projvx=x⋅vv⋅vv=10⋅(−2)+6⋅1+14⋅3(−2)2+12+32v=2[−213]=[−426]projwx=x⋅ww⋅ww=10⋅2+6⋅(−2)+14⋅222+(−2)2+22w=3[2−22]=[6−66]

Therefore, we have that projSx=projvx+projwx=[−426]+[6−66]=[2−412].

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{10\cdot (-2)+6\cdot 1+14\cdot 3}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{10\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}w=3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6 \\ 14\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
question.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$

$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{10\cdot (-2)+6\cdot 1+14\cdot 3}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{10\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}w=3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6 \\ 14\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{10\cdot (-2)+6\cdot 1+14\cdot 3}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{10\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}w=3[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
question.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+4\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{7\cdot (-3)+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-1)[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+4\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{7\cdot (-3)+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-1)[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
question.worked_solution:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+4\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{7\cdot (-3)+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-1)[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S given that the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal.

a

Since the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1}, Span{a2}, and Span{a3}:

proja1x=x⋅a1a1⋅a1a1=7⋅1+3⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅1+4⋅012+(−1)2+12+02a1=[1−110]proja2x=x⋅a2a2⋅a2a2=7⋅1+3⋅1+(−1)⋅0+4⋅212+12+02+22a2=3[1102]proja3x=x⋅a3a3⋅a3a3=7⋅(−3)+3⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅2+4⋅2(−3)2+(−1)2+22+22a2=−[−3−122]

Therefore, we have that

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x=[1−110]+3[1102]+(−1)[−3−122]=[1−110]+[3306]+[31−2−2]=[73−14].

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal.
feedback.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+4\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{7\cdot (-3)+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+(-1)[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the vector x and the subspace S=Span{a1,a2,a3}, where a1=[1−110],a2=[1102],a3=[−3−122],x=[73−14].

Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S given that the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal.

a
 [−3−122]
b
[−3−122]
c
[−1102]
d
 [−1−132]
e
[73−14]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the set {a1,a2,a3} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S is given by

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x.

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of x onto Span{a1}, Span{a2}, and Span{a3}:

proja1x=x⋅a1a1⋅a1a1=7⋅1+3⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅1+4⋅012+(−1)2+12+02a1=[1−110]proja2x=x⋅a2a2⋅a2a2=7⋅1+3⋅1+(−1)⋅0+4⋅212+12+02+22a2=3[1102]proja3x=x⋅a3a3⋅a3a3=7⋅(−3)+3⋅(−1)+(−1)⋅2+4⋅2(−3)2+(−1)2+22+22a2=−[−3−122]

Therefore, we have that

projSx=proja1x+proja2x+proja3x=[1−110]+3[1102]+(−1)[−3−122]=[1−110]+[3306]+[31−2−2]=[73−14].

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $6\times 8$ matrix $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values

II. Any $10\times 8$ matrix $A$ has at most $10$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]$ has two non-negative singular values.
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 8$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $8\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $8\times 8$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{8\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 8}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{8\times 8}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $10\times 8$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $8\times 10$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $8\times 8$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{8\times 10}\times {A}_{10\times 8}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{8\times 8}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $3\times 2$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

II. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -1 & -5\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.

III. Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $2\times 2$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{2\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 2}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{2\times 2}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $1\times4$ matrix $A$ has at most $1$ singular value.

II. Any $4\times2$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14177055/assets/b8601b1e66ef1d302e7194f262f6a513063bba2114fb063c2fc16542d4684392.svg) has one negative singular value.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $1 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 1}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 1} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} =  
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Since $A$ is a $4 \times 2$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ cannot have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Example: 
                    Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
canonical_examples.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14177055/assets/85f9ccea6cd39f07174651d07316218edf50041f9d373e22cdaedf0c779caaf3.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$  

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix
canonical_examples.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14177055/assets/590d5dc32950efa0fce63a5d64a5595210a3ccb08c613e364586dba4822d7314.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$  

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )^{2}-(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14177055/assets/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values.

Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14177055/assets/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

tutorial.content:
Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14177055/assets/27384e999cf503b9c0f827f81fca7ad68451b351edaab53187918687e101e011.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $1 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 1}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 1} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} =  
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Since $A$ is a $4 \times 2$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix: 

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ cannot have a negative singular value.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Singular Values of a Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 8$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $8\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $8\times 8$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{8\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 8}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{8\times 8}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $10\times 8$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $8\times 10$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $8\times 8$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{8\times 10}\times {A}_{10\times 8}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{8\times 8}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $8$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. Any 6×8 matrix A has at most 8 distinct singular values
  2. Any 10×8 matrix A has at most 10 distinct singular values.
  3. The matrix A=[0−1−10] has two non-negative singular values.

b

c
I and III only
d
II and III only

EXPLANATION

The singular values of the matrix A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ATA.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $6\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values.

II. Any $8\times 9$ matrix $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$ has at most two non-negative distinct singular values.
question.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $6\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $8\times 9$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $9\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $9\times 9$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s-3)},\,s>3
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a},\text{ }s>a.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s-3)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-3}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-3}\} \\  & ={e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{3τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{3t}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{24}{{s}^{6}},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{24}{{s}^{6}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{24}{{s}^{5}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{24}{{s}^{5}}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{4!}{{s}^{4+1}}\} \\  & ={t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{4}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s-5)},\,s>5
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a},\text{ }s>a.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s-5)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-5}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-5}\} \\  & ={e}^{5t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{5τ}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5τ}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}({e}^{5t}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{1}{s(s-3)}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-3}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{e}^{at}\}=\frac{1}{s-a}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-3}\} \\  & ={e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$

Notice that we can write G(s) as G(s)=1s(s−3)=F(s)s, where F(s)=1s−3. Also, we know that L{eat}=1s−a. Thus, we get L−1{F(s)}=L−1{1s−3}=e3t.

Question 3
?

For the function G(s)=1s(s−5),s>5 find the inverse Laplace transform of G(s), given that L{eat}=1s−a, s>a.

a
15(et−1)
b
15(e5t−1)
c
1s−5
d
e5t
e
15(1−e5t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that we can write G(s) as G(s)=1s(s−5)=F(s)s, where F(s)=1s−5. Also, we know that L{eat}=1s−a. Thus, we get L−1{F(s)}=L−1{1s−5}=e5t.

Additionally, we know that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{∫0tf(τ)dτ}=F(s)s.

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain L−1{G(s)}=L−1{F(s)s}=∫0tf(τ)dτ=∫0te5τdτ=15e5τ|0t=15(e5t−1).

Suppose we wish to find $L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

question.problem:
Suppose we wish to find $L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ={{field-1}}\,{|}_{0}^{t}=A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={A}^{′}(t)\text{ }dt \\ dv={{field-3}} & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$
