last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 2 \\ -5 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=-2-3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-3\text{i})(1+3\text{i})}{(5)(5)}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

$$

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-3\text{i})(1+3\text{i})}{(5)(5)}=\frac{2}{5}.

{(−1−3i)x1+2x2=0−5x1+(1−3i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(−2+3i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=15(1−3i)x2

Hence, the general solution is given by

[15(1−3i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=5, we get the eigenvector

v1=[1−3i5].

On the other hand, since λ1=−2+3i is a complex eigenvalue of A, the second eigenvalue of A must be the complex conjugate of λ1. Therefore,

λ2=λ1―=−2−3i.

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to λ2 is

v2=v―1=[1+3i5].

Therefore, we obtain

a1a2b1b2=(1−3i)(1+3i)(5)(5)=25.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2+\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3-\text{i} & -2 \\ 5 & 3-\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-3-\text{i}){x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-5}{3-\text{i}}=\frac{-5(3+\text{i})}{10}=-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[−5−251] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=−2+i, then what is the value of ba?

Now, since the matrix A−(−2+i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=−15(3−i)x2

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[−15(3−i)x2x2],x2∈C.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2+\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3-\text{i} & -2 \\ 5 & 3-\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-3-\text{i}){x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-5}{3-\text{i}}=\frac{-5(3+\text{i})}{10}=-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$

Question 3
?

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[−5−251] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=−2+i, then what is the value of ba?

a

b
32+i
c

d

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=−2+i, and

A−λI=[−5−251]−[−2+i00−2+i]=[−3−i−253−i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(−3−i)x1−2x2=05x1+(3−i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−(−2+i)I is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=−15(3−i)x2

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[−15(3−i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=−5, we get the eigenvector

v=[3−i−5].

Finally, ba=−53−i=−5(3+i)10=−32−12i.

feedback.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2+\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3-\text{i} & -2 \\ 5 & 3-\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-3-\text{i}){x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}(3-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3-\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-5}{3-\text{i}}=\frac{-5(3+\text{i})}{10}=-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{5}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{5}\text{i} \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-3}{2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}}=\frac{-3(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i})}{9}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\text{i}.$

Question 5
?

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[23−3−2] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=5i, then what is the value of ba?

a
32
b
53−23i
c
−23−53i
d
−23+53i
e
−53+23i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=5i, and

A−λI=[23−3−2]−[5i005i]=[2−5i3−3−2−5i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(2−5i)x1+3x2=0−3x1+(−2−5i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−5iI is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=−13(2+5i)x2

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[−13(2+5i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=−3, we get the eigenvector

v=[2+5i−3].

Finally, ba=−32+5i=−3(2−5i)9=−23+53i.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{5}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{5}\text{i} \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-3}{2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}}=\frac{-3(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i})}{9}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\text{i}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$

question.html:
Question 5
?

If v=[ab] is an eigenvector of A=[23−3−2] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=5i, then what is the value of ba?

a
32
b
53−23i
c
−23−53i
d
−23+53i
e
−53+23i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=5i, and

A−λI=[23−3−2]−[5i005i]=[2−5i3−3−2−5i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(2−5i)x1+3x2=0−3x1+(−2−5i)x2=0.

Now, since the matrix A−5iI is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

x1=−13(2+5i)x2

Therefore, the general solution is given by

[−13(2+5i)x2x2],x2∈C.

Setting x2=−3, we get the eigenvector

v=[2+5i−3].

Finally, ba=−32+5i=−3(2−5i)9=−23+53i.

solution.reasoning: The first row of Av=λv gives 2a+3b=√5 i a, hence b/a=(−2+√5 i)/3. The component a is nonzero because a=0 would force b=0. Therefore option d is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer-key evidence is captured.

feedback.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =\sqrt{5}\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-\sqrt{5}\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & -2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+(-2-\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-\sqrt{5}\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}(2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2+\sqrt{5}\text{i} \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-3}{2+\sqrt{5}\text{i}}=\frac{-3(2-\sqrt{5}\text{i})}{9}=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\text{i}.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $-\frac{1}{7}=\frac{(-1)}{7}.$

To raise the fraction to the power of $2$, we must raise both the numerator and the denominator to the power of $2:$

$$
{(-\frac{1}{7})}^{2}={(\frac{(-1)}{7})}^{2}=\frac{(-1)^{2}}{{7}^{2}}
$$

Now, using $(-1)^{2}=1$ and ${7}^{2}=49,$ we get

$$
\frac{(-1)^{2}}{{7}^{2}}=\frac{1}{49}.
$$

$$
\frac{{1}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}=\frac{1}{8}.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that $-\frac{1}{7}=\frac{(-1)}{7}.$

To raise the fraction to the power of $2$, we must raise both the numerator and the denominator to the power of $2:$

$$
{(-\frac{1}{7})}^{2}={(\frac{(-1)}{7})}^{2}=\frac{(-1)^{2}}{{7}^{2}}
$$

Now, using $(-1)^{2}=1$ and ${7}^{2}=49,$ we get

$$
\frac{(-1)^{2}}{{7}^{2}}=\frac{1}{49}.
$$

$$
\frac{{1}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}=\frac{1}{8}.

To raise the fraction to the power of $2$, we must raise both the numerator and the denominator to the power of $2:$

$$
{(-\frac{1}{7})}^{2}={(\frac{(-1)}{7})}^{2}=\frac{(-1)^{2}}{{7}^{2}}
$$

$$
\frac{(-1)^{2}}{{7}^{2}}=\frac{1}{49}.

Question 3
?

(−17)2=

a
−17
b
−114
c
17
d
−149
e
149
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that −17=(−1)7.

To raise the fraction to the power of 2, we must raise both the numerator and the denominator to the power of 2:

(−17)2=((−1)7)2=(−1)272

Now, using (−1)2=1 and 72=49, we get

(−1)272=149.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that $-\frac{1}{7}=\frac{(-1)}{7}.$

To raise the fraction to the power of $2$, we must raise both the numerator and the denominator to the power of $2:$

$$
{(-\frac{1}{7})}^{2}={(\frac{(-1)}{7})}^{2}=\frac{(-1)^{2}}{{7}^{2}}
$$

Now, using $(-1)^{2}=1$ and ${7}^{2}=49,$ we get

$$
\frac{(-1)^{2}}{{7}^{2}}=\frac{1}{49}.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $C=\{[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,|\,a\in R\}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $C$ is closed under matrix addition

II. $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $C$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

IV. $C$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ are two matrices from $C,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $C.$ So, $C$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $A=[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ is an element of $C$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}ka & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $C.$ So, $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $C$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of all continuous functions $f:[-1,1]\to R$ and its subset $B=\{f\in C[-1,1]\,|\,f(1)=f(-1)\}.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $B$ is closed under function addition

II. $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $B$ is a subspace of $C[-1,1]$

IV. $B$ is **not** a subspace of $C[-1,1]$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(x),g(x)\in B,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(1) & =f(1)+g(1) \\  & =f(-1)+g(-1) \\  & =(f+g)(-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, $B$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(x)\in B$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}(kf)(1) & =kf(1) \\  & =kf(-1) \\  & =(kf)(-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $B$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the vector space $C[0,3]$ of all continuous functions $f:[0,3]\to R$ and its subset $N$ containing all functions that return a nonzero value at exactly one point in $[0,3].$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $N$ is closed under function addition

II. $N$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $N$ is a subspace of $C[0,3]$

IV. $N$ is **not** a subspace of $C[0,3]$

*Hint: Different functions from $N$ might give a nonzero value at different points in $[0,3].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if $f({a}_{1})\ne 0$ and $g({a}_{2})\ne 0,$ where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ are distinct points in $[0,3],$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f({a}_{1})+g({a}_{1}) & \ne 0 \\ f({a}_{2})+g({a}_{2}) & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)+g(x)\ne 0$ at two distinct points. So, $N$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(a)\ne 0$ for some $a\in [0,3],$ and $k=0,$ then

$$
kf(x)=0
$$

 
for any $x\in [0,3].$ So, $N$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $N$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the vector space $C[-2,2]$ of all continuous functions $f:[-2,2]\to R$ and its subset $E$ containing all even functions.

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $E$ is closed under function addition

II. $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $E$ is a subspace of $C[-2,2]$

IV. $E$ is **not** a subspace of $C[-2,2]$

*Hint: $f$ is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ for all $x\in [-2,2].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(x),g(x)\in E,$ then

$$

$$

$$
kf(x)=0
$$

 
for any $x\in [0,3].$ So, $N$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $N$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."

links.title: Computing Partial Derivatives Using the Rules of Differentiation

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y})?$

I. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$

II. ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that $f$ is defined only when

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}>0.
$$

At points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1+1})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}),
$$

and both partial derivatives are defined there:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\frac{1}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{0}{0+1}=0,
$$

so

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.

- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(-1,1,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{yz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{yz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xy}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xy{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I  only'.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Given that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂z}=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} & ={D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $y$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$

II. ${f}_{x}(0,1,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,-1,1)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1,0)=0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡((-1)\cdot (-1))=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1,0) & =\frac{0}{(-1)}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,-1,1)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,-1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot (-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1),
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we note that $f$ is defined only when

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}>0.
$$

At points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1+1})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}),
$$

and both partial derivatives are defined there:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\frac{1}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{0}{0+1}=0,
$$

so

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.

- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Question 1
?

Which of the following statements are true about the function f(x,y)=ln⁡(xx+y)?

  1. Both partial derivatives exist at the point (1,1)
  2. fx(0,1) is defined
  3. fy(0,1) is defined
a
I only
b
I, II, and III
c
I and III only
d
I and II only
e
II only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that f is defined only when xx+y>0.

At points in the domain of f, we can compute the partial derivatives: fx(x,y)=∂∂xln⁡(xx+y)=x+yx⋅∂∂x(xx+y)=x+yx⋅1⋅(x+y)−x⋅1(x+y)2=x+yx⋅y(x+y)2=yx(x+y)fy(x,y)=∂∂yln⁡(xx+y)=x+yx⋅∂∂y(xx+y)=x+yx⋅(−x(x+y)2)=−1x+y.

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

  • Statement I is true. The function is defined at (1,1), since f(1,1)=ln⁡(11+1)=ln⁡(12), and both partial derivatives are defined there: fx(1,1)=11(1+1)=12fy(1,1)=−11+1=−12.

  • Statement II is false. At (0,1), xx+y=00+1=0, so f(0,1)=ln⁡(0), which is undefined. Therefore, fx(0,1) is not defined.

  • Statement III is false for the same reason. Since f is not defined at (0,1), the partial derivative fy(0,1) is not defined. The simplified expression −1x+y cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of f.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{yz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{yz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xy}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xy{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I  only'.

f(1,-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I  only'.

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

$$

$$

$$

Question 3
?

Given that g(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z and ∂g∂x=2xz(x2+y2−1),∂g∂y=2yz(x2+y2−1),∂g∂z=−ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z2, find the set of values (x,y,z) where all partial derivatives of g exist.

a
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}
b
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>0,z>0}
c
{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1}
d
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1}
e
{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that g(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z is defined only when x2+y2−1>0 and z≠0. So, the domain of g is Dg={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}.

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function gx(x,y,z)=2xz(x2+y2−1) is defined only when x2+y2−1≠0 and z≠0. So, the domain of gx is Dgx={(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}.

  • Similarly, the domain of gy(x,y,z) is the same: Dgy=Dgx={(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}.

  • The function gz(x,y,z)=−ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z2 is defined only when x2+y2−1>0 and z≠0. So, the domain of gz is Dgz={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}.

Finally, we conclude that the partials of g exist on the set

Dg∩Dgx∩Dgy∩Dgz=Dg∩Dgx∩Dgz={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}=∩{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}=∩{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$

a
{(x,y,z):x≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z
b
{(x,y,z):y>0,z≠0}

{(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠0}

First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1,0)=0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡((-1)\cdot (-1))=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1,0) & =\frac{0}{(-1)}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{0},

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,-1,1)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,-1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot (-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1),
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y})?$

I. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$

II. ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that $f$ is defined only when

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}>0.
$$

At points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1+1})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}),
$$

and both partial derivatives are defined there:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\frac{1}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{0}{0+1}=0,
$$

so

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.

- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(-1,1,1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined
question.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{yz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{yz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xy}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xy{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I  only'.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂z}=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist.
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} & ={D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given that g(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z and ∂g∂x=2xz(x2+y2−1),∂g∂y=2yz(x2+y2−1),∂g∂z=−ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z2, find the set of values (x,y,z) where all partial derivatives of g exist.

a
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}
b
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>0,z>0}
c
{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1}
d
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1}
e
{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that g(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z is defined only when x2+y2−1>0 and z≠0. So, the domain of g is Dg={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}.

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function gx(x,y,z)=2xz(x2+y2−1) is defined only when x2+y2−1≠0 and z≠0. So, the domain of gx is Dgx={(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}.

  • Similarly, the domain of gy(x,y,z) is the same: Dgy=Dgx={(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}.

  • The function gz(x,y,z)=−ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z2 is defined only when x2+y2−1>0 and z≠0. So, the domain of gz is Dgz={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}.

Finally, we conclude that the partials of g exist on the set

Dg∩Dgx∩Dgy∩Dgz=Dg∩Dgx∩Dgz={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}=∩{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}=∩{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} & ={D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ and

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that g(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z and ∂g∂x=2xz(x2+y2−1),∂g∂y=2yz(x2+y2−1),∂g∂z=−ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z2, find the set of values (x,y,z) where all partial derivatives of g exist.

a
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}
b
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>0,z>0}
c
{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1}
d
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1}
e
{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that g(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z is defined only when x2+y2−1>0 and z≠0. So, the domain of g is Dg={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}.

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function gx(x,y,z)=2xz(x2+y2−1) is defined only when x2+y2−1≠0 and z≠0. So, the domain of gx is Dgx={(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}.

  • Similarly, the domain of gy(x,y,z) is the same: Dgy=Dgx={(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}.

  • The function gz(x,y,z)=−ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z2 is defined only when x2+y2−1>0 and z≠0. So, the domain of gz is Dgz={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}.

Finally, we conclude that the partials of g exist on the set

Dg∩Dgx∩Dgy∩Dgz=Dg∩Dgx∩Dgz={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}=∩{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}=∩{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}

solution.reasoning: The real logarithm requires x²+y²−1>0, and division by z requires z≠0. On this open domain, all three supplied partial derivatives are defined. Outside it, g itself is undefined, so its partial derivatives cannot exist. The mathematical answer is option a; no Math Academy answer-key evidence was provided.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Given that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂z}=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} & ={D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given that g(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z and ∂g∂x=2xz(x2+y2−1),∂g∂y=2yz(x2+y2−1),∂g∂z=−ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z2, find the set of values (x,y,z) where all partial derivatives of g exist.

a
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}
b
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>0,z>0}
c
{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1}
d
{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1}
e
{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that g(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z is defined only when x2+y2−1>0 and z≠0. So, the domain of g is Dg={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}.

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function gx(x,y,z)=2xz(x2+y2−1) is defined only when x2+y2−1≠0 and z≠0. So, the domain of gx is Dgx={(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}.

  • Similarly, the domain of gy(x,y,z) is the same: Dgy=Dgx={(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}.

  • The function gz(x,y,z)=−ln⁡(x2+y2−1)z2 is defined only when x2+y2−1>0 and z≠0. So, the domain of gz is Dgz={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}.

Finally, we conclude that the partials of g exist on the set

Dg∩Dgx∩Dgy∩Dgz=Dg∩Dgx∩Dgz={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}=∩{(x,y,z):x2+y2≠1,z≠0}=∩{(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}={(x,y,z):x2+y2>1,z≠0}

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Given that f(x,y,z)=xysin⁡z and ∂f∂x=1ysin⁡z,∂f∂y=−xy2sin⁡z,∂f∂z=−xcos⁡zysin2⁡z find the set of values (x,y,z) where all partial derivatives of f exist.

a
{(x,y,z):x≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z
b
{(x,y,z):y>0,z≠0}
c
{(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠0}
d
{(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z
e
{(x,y,z):y>0,z≠nπ},n∈Z
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that f(x,y,z)=xysin⁡z is defined only when y≠0 and z≠nπ where n∈Z. So, the domain of f is Df={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z.

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function fx(x,y,z)=1ysin⁡z is defined only when y≠0 and z≠nπ where n∈Z. So, the domain of fx is Dfx={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z.

  • Similarly, the domains of fy and fz are the same: Dfy=Dfz={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z.

Finally, we conclude that the partials of f exist on the set

Df∩Dfx∩Dfy∩Dfz=Df∩Dfx={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ}∩{(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ}={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$

{(x,y,z):x≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z
b
{(x,y,z):y>0,z≠0}
c
{(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠0}
d
{(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z
e
{(x,y,z):y>0,z≠nπ},n∈Z
Submit

EXPLANATION

First, notice that f(x,y,z)=xysin⁡z is defined only when y≠0 and z≠nπ where n∈Z. So, the domain of f is Df={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z.

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function fx(x,y,z)=1ysin⁡z is defined only when y≠0 and z≠nπ where n∈Z. So, the domain of fx is Dfx={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z.

  • Similarly, the domains of fy and fz are the same: Dfy=Dfz={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z.

Finally, we conclude that the partials of f exist on the set

Df∩Dfx∩Dfy∩Dfz=Df∩Dfx={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ}∩{(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ}={(x,y,z):y≠0,z≠nπ},n∈Z.

solution.reasoning: All partial derivatives exist wherever y≠0 and sin z≠0, equivalently z≠nπ for every integer n. There is no restriction on x. This is an open domain where f is smooth; elsewhere f is undefined. Thus option d is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was provided.

feedback.problem:
Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$

III. ${f}_{z}(1,-1,1)$ is defined
question.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{z}{y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}z\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(z) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1,0)=0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡((-1)\cdot (-1))=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1,0) & =\frac{0}{(-1)}=0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,-1,1)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,-1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot (-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1),
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

We divide and multiply, from left to right:

$$
\begin{aligned}2÷\frac{2}{5}\times 4 & = \\ (2÷\frac{2}{5})\times 4 & = \\ (2\times \frac{5}{2})\times 4 & = \\ (\frac{2}{1}\times \frac{5}{2})\times 4 & = \\ \frac{2\times 5}{1\times 2}\times 4 & = \\ \frac{\cancel{2}\times 5}{1\times \cancel{2}}\times 4 & = \\ 5\times 4 & = \\ 20\end{aligned}
$$

First, we perform the operation inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\times (2.3-0.1) & = \\ (-4)\times 2.2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\times 2.2 & =-8.8\end{aligned}

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7|2x-5|+1 & =15 \\ 7|2x-5| & =14 \\ |2x-5| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|2x-5|=2x-5,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ 2x-5 & =2 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|2x-5|=-(2x-5),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ -(2x-5) & =2 \\ -2x+5 & =2 \\ -2x & =-3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\frac{3}{2}$ and $x=\frac{7}{2}.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Which of the following equations has *no* solution?

I. $|5z+1|=5$

II. $|5z+1|-3=-1$

III. $|5z+1|=-6$
questions.worked_solution:
An absolute value equation has no solution if, when the absolute value is isolated on the left side, the right-hand side is negative.

With that in mind, let's look at each equation in turn:

- Equation I has a solution. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is non-negative.

- Equation II has a solution. To see this, we first isolate the absolute value on the left-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5z+1|-3 & =-1 \\ |5z+1| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Since the right-hand side is non-negative, this equation has a solution.

- Equation III *has no solution*. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is *negative*.

Therefore, the answer is "III only."

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7|2x-5|+1 & =15 \\ 7|2x-5| & =14 \\ |2x-5| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|2x-5|=2x-5,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ 2x-5 & =2 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|2x-5|=-(2x-5),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ -(2x-5) & =2 \\ -2x+5 & =2 \\ -2x & =-3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\frac{3}{2}$ and $x=\frac{7}{2}.$

question.name: Question 1
question.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7|2x-5|+1 & =15 \\ 7|2x-5| & =14 \\ |2x-5| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|2x-5|=2x-5,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ 2x-5 & =2 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|2x-5|=-(2x-5),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ -(2x-5) & =2 \\ -2x+5 & =2 \\ -2x & =-3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}

Question 1
?

If 7|2x−5|+1=15, then x=

a
x=32,7
b
x=−32,72
c
x=3,72
d
x=32,72
e
x=−72,23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation: 7|2x−5|+1=157|2x−5|=14|2x−5|=2

Now, we have the following two cases:

  • If |2x−5|=2x−5, we obtain: |2x−5|=22x−5=22x=7x=72

  • If |2x−5|=−(2x−5), we obtain: |2x−5|=2−(2x−5)=2−2x+5=2−2x=−3x=32

Therefore, the solutions are x=32 and x=72.

question.html:
Question 1
?

If 7|2x−5|+1=15, then x=

a
x=32,7
b
x=−32,72
c
x=3,72
d
x=32,72
e
x=−72,23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation: 7|2x−5|+1=157|2x−5|=14|2x−5|=2

Now, we have the following two cases:

  • If |2x−5|=2x−5, we obtain: |2x−5|=22x−5=22x=7x=72

  • If |2x−5|=−(2x−5), we obtain: |2x−5|=2−(2x−5)=2−2x+5=2−2x=−3x=32

Therefore, the solutions are x=32 and x=72.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7|2x-5|+1 & =15 \\ 7|2x-5| & =14 \\ |2x-5| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|2x-5|=2x-5,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ 2x-5 & =2 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|2x-5|=-(2x-5),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x-5| & =2 \\ -(2x-5) & =2 \\ -2x+5 & =2 \\ -2x & =-3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\frac{3}{2}$ and $x=\frac{7}{2}.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Which of the following equations has *no* solution?

I. $|5z+1|=5$

II. $|5z+1|-3=-1$

III. $|5z+1|=-6$
question.worked_solution:
An absolute value equation has no solution if, when the absolute value is isolated on the left side, the right-hand side is negative.

With that in mind, let's look at each equation in turn:

- Equation I has a solution. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is non-negative.

- Equation II has a solution. To see this, we first isolate the absolute value on the left-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|5z+1|-3 & =-1 \\ |5z+1| & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Since the right-hand side is non-negative, this equation has a solution.

- Equation III *has no solution*. The absolute value is already isolated on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is *negative*.

Therefore, the answer is "III only."

Therefore, the answer is "III only."

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}-z$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,e).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }k \\  & ={e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j-k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,e) & ={e}^{1}\text{ }i+(1){e}^{1}\text{ }j-k \\  & =e\,i+e\,j-k \\  & =⟨e,e,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨e,e,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Consider the surface ${x}^{2}=-xyz.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(4,2,-2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =-xyz \\ {x}^{2}+xyz & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

 

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,2,-2) & =(2(4)+2(-2))\text{ }i+4(-2)\text{ }j+4(2)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i-8j+8\,k \\  & =⟨4,-8,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,2,-2)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,-8,8⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-4)+(-8)(y-2)+8(z+2) & =0 \\ 4x-8y+8z+16 & =0 \\ x-2y+2z+4=0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-{e}^{z}\text{ }j-y{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,2,1) & =\frac{2}{1}\text{ }i-{e}^{1}\text{ }j-(2){e}^{1}k \\  & =2\,i-e\,j-2ek \\  & =⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes  through the point where $(x,y,z)=(\frac{1}{2},3,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(\frac{1}{2},3,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }k \\  & =12x\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3{z}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(\frac{1}{2},3,2) & =12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3(2)^{2}k \\  & =6\,i-\,j+12k \\  & =⟨6,-1,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},3,2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨6,-1,12⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 6(x-\frac{1}{2})-(y-3)+12(z-2) & =0 \\ 6x-y+12z-24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Consider the surface $xy{z}^{2}=6-z.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(1,1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{z}^{2} & =6-z \\ xy{z}^{2}+z & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =(y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+(x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2xyz+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,2) & =(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }i+(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i+4j+5\,k \\  & =⟨4,4,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,4,5⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-1)+4(y-1)+5(z-2) & =0 \\ 4x+4y+5z-18 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given the function f(x,y,z)=xey−z, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,e).

a
⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
b
⟨1,1,−e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
c
⟨1,1,e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
d
⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+1,z+e⟩=0
e
⟨1,1,−e⟩⋅⟨x−e,y−e,z−1⟩=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(1,1,e):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(xey−z) i+∂∂y(xey−z) j+∂∂z(xey−z) k=ey i+xey j−k∇f(1,1,e)=e1 i+(1)e1 j−k=ei+ej−k=⟨e,e,−1⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,1,e)⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =-xyz \\ {x}^{2}+xyz & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

 

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,2,-2) & =(2(4)+2(-2))\text{ }i+4(-2)\text{ }j+4(2)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i-8j+8\,k \\  & =⟨4,-8,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,2,-2)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,-8,8⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-4)+(-8)(y-2)+8(z+2) & =0 \\ 4x-8y+8z+16 & =0 \\ x-2y+2z+4=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

 

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,2,-2) & =(2(4)+2(-2))\text{ }i+4(-2)\text{ }j+4(2)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i-8j+8\,k \\  & =⟨4,-8,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,2,-2)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,-8,8⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-4)+(-8)(y-2)+8(z+2) & =0 \\ 4x-8y+8z+16 & =0 \\ x-2y+2z+4=0\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-{e}^{z}\text{ }j-y{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,2,1) & =\frac{2}{1}\text{ }i-{e}^{1}\text{ }j-(2){e}^{1}k \\  & =2\,i-e\,j-2ek \\  & =⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given the function f(x,y,z)=2ln⁡x−yez, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,2,1).

a
 ⟨2,e,2e⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+2,z+1⟩=0
b
 ⟨1,e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
c
 ⟨e,1,2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
d
 ⟨2,e,−e⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+2,z+1⟩=0
e
 ⟨2,−e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(1,2,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(2ln⁡x−yez) i+∂∂y(2ln⁡x−yez) j+∂∂z(2ln⁡x−yez k=2x i−ez j−yezk∇f(1,2,1)=21 i−e1 j−(2)e1k=2i−ej−2ek=⟨2,−e,−2e⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,2,1)⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0⟨2,−e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(\frac{1}{2},3,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }k \\  & =12x\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3{z}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(\frac{1}{2},3,2) & =12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3(2)^{2}k \\  & =6\,i-\,j+12k \\  & =⟨6,-1,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},3,2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨6,-1,12⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 6(x-\frac{1}{2})-(y-3)+12(z-2) & =0 \\ 6x-y+12z-24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Given the function f(x,y,z)=6x2−y+z3, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(12,3,2).

a
 6x−y+z+12=0
b
 3x−2y−5z+11=0
c
 6x−3y−4z+24=0
d
 2x−y−4z+13=0
e
 6x−y+12z−24=0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(12,3,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(6x2−y+z3) i+∂∂y(6x2−y+z3) j+∂∂z(6x2−y+z3) k=12x i− j+3z2k∇f(12,3,2)=12⋅12 i− j+3(2)2k=6i−j+12k=⟨6,−1,12⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(12,3,2)⋅⟨x−12,y−3,z−2⟩=0⟨6,−1,12⟩⋅⟨x−12,y−3,z−2⟩=06(x−12)−(y−3)+12(z−2)=06x−y+12z−24=0

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{z}^{2} & =6-z \\ xy{z}^{2}+z & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =(y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+(x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2xyz+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,2) & =(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }i+(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i+4j+5\,k \\  & =⟨4,4,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,4,5⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-1)+4(y-1)+5(z-2) & =0 \\ 4x+4y+5z-18 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Consider the surface $xy{z}^{2}=6-z.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(1,1,2).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{z}^{2} & =6-z \\ xy{z}^{2}+z & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =(y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+(x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2xyz+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,2) & =(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }i+(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i+4j+5\,k \\  & =⟨4,4,5⟩\end{aligned}
