Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,4,5⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-1)+4(y-1)+5(z-2) & =0 \\ 4x+4y+5z-18 & =0\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the surface xyz2=6−z. Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point (1,1,2).

a
 4x+4y+5z−18=0
b
 4x−y+2z−10=0
c
 4x+3y+z+12=0
d
 x+4y−3z+15=0
e
 2x−y+5z−12=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

xyz2=6−zxyz2+z=6

If we set f(x,y,z)=xyz2+z, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=6.

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

Now, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (1,1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(xyz2+z) i+∂∂y(xyz2+z) j+∂∂z(xyz2+z) k=(yz2) i+(xz2) j+(2xyz+1) k∇f(1,1,2)=(1)(2)2 i+(1)(2)2 j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1) k=4i+4j+5k=⟨4,4,5⟩

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,1,2)⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−2⟩=0⟨4,4,5⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−2⟩=04(x−1)+4(y−1)+5(z−2)=04x+4y+5z−18=0

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}-z$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,e).$
question.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }k \\  & ={e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j-k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,e) & ={e}^{1}\text{ }i+(1){e}^{1}\text{ }j-k \\  & =e\,i+e\,j-k \\  & =⟨e,e,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨e,e,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Given the function f(x,y,z)=xey−z, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,e).

a
⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
b
⟨1,1,−e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
c
⟨1,1,e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
d
⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+1,z+e⟩=0
e
⟨1,1,−e⟩⋅⟨x−e,y−e,z−1⟩=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(1,1,e):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(xey−z) i+∂∂y(xey−z) j+∂∂z(xey−z) k=ey i+xey j−k∇f(1,1,e)=e1 i+(1)e1 j−k=ei+ej−k=⟨e,e,−1⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,1,e)⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }k \\  & ={e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j-k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,e) & ={e}^{1}\text{ }i+(1){e}^{1}\text{ }j-k \\  & =e\,i+e\,j-k \\  & =⟨e,e,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨e,e,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Given the function f(x,y,z)=xey−z, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,1,e).

a
⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
b
⟨1,1,−e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
c
⟨1,1,e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0
d
⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+1,z+e⟩=0
e
⟨1,1,−e⟩⋅⟨x−e,y−e,z−1⟩=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(1,1,e):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(xey−z) i+∂∂y(xey−z) j+∂∂z(xey−z) k=ey i+xey j−k∇f(1,1,e)=e1 i+(1)e1 j−k=ei+ej−k=⟨e,e,−1⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,1,e)⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0

solution.reasoning: The gradient is \nabla f=(e^y,xe^y,-1), so at (1,1,e) it is (e,e,-1). This nonzero vector is normal to the level surface. Thus the tangent plane is e(x-1)+e(y-1)-(z-e)=0, matching option a. Mathematical correctness is clear, but no captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}-z$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,e).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}-z)\text{ }k \\  & ={e}^{y}\text{ }i+x{e}^{y}\text{ }j-k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,e) & ={e}^{1}\text{ }i+(1){e}^{1}\text{ }j-k \\  & =e\,i+e\,j-k \\  & =⟨e,e,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨e,e,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-e⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(1,1,e):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(xey−z) i+∂∂y(xey−z) j+∂∂z(xey−z) k=ey i+xey j−k∇f(1,1,e)=e1 i+(1)e1 j−k=ei+ej−k=⟨e,e,−1⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,1,e)⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0⟨e,e,−1⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−e⟩=0

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Consider the surface ${x}^{2}=-xyz.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(4,2,-2).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =-xyz \\ {x}^{2}+xyz & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

 

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,2,-2) & =(2(4)+2(-2))\text{ }i+4(-2)\text{ }j+4(2)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i-8j+8\,k \\  & =⟨4,-8,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,2,-2)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,-8,8⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-4)+(-8)(y-2)+8(z+2) & =0 \\ 4x-8y+8z+16 & =0 \\ x-2y+2z+4=0\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =-xyz \\ {x}^{2}+xyz & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

 

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,2,-2) & =(2(4)+2(-2))\text{ }i+4(-2)\text{ }j+4(2)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i-8j+8\,k \\  & =⟨4,-8,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,2,-2)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,-8,8⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-4)+(-8)(y-2)+8(z+2) & =0 \\ 4x-8y+8z+16 & =0 \\ x-2y+2z+4=0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Consider the surface x2=−xyz. Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point (4,2,−2).

a
x+2y−2z−12=0
b
x−2y+2z+4=0
c
2x−y+z−4=0
d
x−4y+z+6=0
e
x−2y+2z−8=0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

x2=−xyzx2+xyz=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=x2+xyz, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

Now, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (4,2,−2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(x2+xyz) i+∂∂y(x2+xyz) j+∂∂z(x2+xyz) k=(2x+yz) i+xz j+xy k∇f(4,2,−2)=(2(4)+2(−2)) i+4(−2) j+4(2) k=4i−8j+8k=⟨4,−8,8⟩

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(4,2,−2)⋅⟨x−4,y−2,z+2⟩=0⟨4,−8,8⟩⋅⟨x−4,y−2,z+2⟩=04(x−4)+(−8)(y−2)+8(z+2)=04x−8y+8z+16=0x−2y+2z+4=0

feedback.problem: Consider the surface ${x}^{2}=-xyz.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(4,2,-2).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =-xyz \\ {x}^{2}+xyz & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

 

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(4,2,-2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(4,2,-2) & =(2(4)+2(-2))\text{ }i+4(-2)\text{ }j+4(2)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i-8j+8\,k \\  & =⟨4,-8,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(4,2,-2)\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,-8,8⟩\cdot ⟨x-4,\,y-2,\,z+2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-4)+(-8)(y-2)+8(z+2) & =0 \\ 4x-8y+8z+16 & =0 \\ x-2y+2z+4=0\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,2,1).$
question.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-{e}^{z}\text{ }j-y{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,2,1) & =\frac{2}{1}\text{ }i-{e}^{1}\text{ }j-(2){e}^{1}k \\  & =2\,i-e\,j-2ek \\  & =⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given the function f(x,y,z)=2ln⁡x−yez, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,2,1).

a
 ⟨2,e,2e⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+2,z+1⟩=0
b
 ⟨1,e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
c
 ⟨e,1,2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
d
 ⟨2,e,−e⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+2,z+1⟩=0
e
 ⟨2,−e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(1,2,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(2ln⁡x−yez) i+∂∂y(2ln⁡x−yez) j+∂∂z(2ln⁡x−yez k=2x i−ez j−yezk∇f(1,2,1)=21 i−e1 j−(2)e1k=2i−ej−2ek=⟨2,−e,−2e⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,2,1)⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0⟨2,−e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-{e}^{z}\text{ }j-y{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,2,1) & =\frac{2}{1}\text{ }i-{e}^{1}\text{ }j-(2){e}^{1}k \\  & =2\,i-e\,j-2ek \\  & =⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given the function f(x,y,z)=2ln⁡x−yez, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,2,1).

a
 ⟨2,e,2e⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+2,z+1⟩=0
b
 ⟨1,e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
c
 ⟨e,1,2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
d
 ⟨2,e,−e⟩⋅⟨x+1,y+2,z+1⟩=0
e
 ⟨2,−e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(1,2,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(2ln⁡x−yez) i+∂∂y(2ln⁡x−yez) j+∂∂z(2ln⁡x−yez k=2x i−ez j−yezk∇f(1,2,1)=21 i−e1 j−(2)e1k=2i−ej−2ek=⟨2,−e,−2e⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,2,1)⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0⟨2,−e,−2e⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−2,z−1⟩=0

solution.reasoning: The gradient is \nabla f=(2/x,-e^z,-ye^z), which equals (2,-e,-2e) at (1,2,1). This nonzero normal gives the tangent plane 2(x-1)-e(y-2)-2e(z-1)=0, matching option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,2,1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y{e}^{z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-{e}^{z}\text{ }j-y{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,2,1) & =\frac{2}{1}\text{ }i-{e}^{1}\text{ }j-(2){e}^{1}k \\  & =2\,i-e\,j-2ek \\  & =⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2,-e,-2e⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-2,\,z-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes  through the point where $(x,y,z)=(\frac{1}{2},3,2).$
question.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(\frac{1}{2},3,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }k \\  & =12x\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3{z}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(\frac{1}{2},3,2) & =12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3(2)^{2}k \\  & =6\,i-\,j+12k \\  & =⟨6,-1,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},3,2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨6,-1,12⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 6(x-\frac{1}{2})-(y-3)+12(z-2) & =0 \\ 6x-y+12z-24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Given the function f(x,y,z)=6x2−y+z3, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(12,3,2).

a
 6x−y+z+12=0
b
 3x−2y−5z+11=0
c
 6x−3y−4z+24=0
d
 2x−y−4z+13=0
e
 6x−y+12z−24=0

Incorrect

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

First, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x0,y0,z0)=(12,3,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(6x2−y+z3) i+∂∂y(6x2−y+z3) j+∂∂z(6x2−y+z3) k=12x i− j+3z2k∇f(12,3,2)=12⋅12 i− j+3(2)2k=6i−j+12k=⟨6,−1,12⟩

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(12,3,2)⋅⟨x−12,y−3,z−2⟩=0⟨6,−1,12⟩⋅⟨x−12,y−3,z−2⟩=06(x−12)−(y−3)+12(z−2)=06x−y+12z−24=0

The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(\frac{1}{2},3,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }k \\  & =12x\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3{z}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(\frac{1}{2},3,2) & =12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3(2)^{2}k \\  & =6\,i-\,j+12k \\  & =⟨6,-1,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},3,2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨6,-1,12⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 6(x-\frac{1}{2})-(y-3)+12(z-2) & =0 \\ 6x-y+12z-24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

feedback.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)=6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes  through the point where $(x,y,z)=(\frac{1}{2},3,2).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(\frac{1}{2},3,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}-y+{z}^{3})\text{ }k \\  & =12x\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3{z}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(\frac{1}{2},3,2) & =12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{ }i-\text{ }j+3(2)^{2}k \\  & =6\,i-\,j+12k \\  & =⟨6,-1,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},3,2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨6,-1,12⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{1}{2},\,y-3,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 6(x-\frac{1}{2})-(y-3)+12(z-2) & =0 \\ 6x-y+12z-24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Consider the surface $xy{z}^{2}=6-z.$ Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point $(1,1,2).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{z}^{2} & =6-z \\ xy{z}^{2}+z & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{z}^{2}+z)\text{ }k \\  & =(y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+(x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2xyz+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,2) & =(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }i+(1)(2)^{2}\text{ }j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1)\text{ }k \\  & =4\,i+4j+5\,k \\  & =⟨4,4,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨4,4,5⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z-2⟩ & =0 \\ 4(x-1)+4(y-1)+5(z-2) & =0 \\ 4x+4y+5z-18 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the surface xyz2=6−z. Find the equation of the tangent plane to that surface at the point (1,1,2).

a
 4x+4y+5z−18=0
b
 4x−y+2z−10=0
c
 4x+3y+z+12=0
d
 x+4y−3z+15=0
e
 2x−y+5z−12=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

xyz2=6−zxyz2+z=6

If we set f(x,y,z)=xyz2+z, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=6.

Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface f(x,y,z)=k at the point (x0,y0,z0) can be expressed as

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0.

Now, we find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (1,1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z)j+fz(x,y,z)k=∂∂x(xyz2+z) i+∂∂y(xyz2+z) j+∂∂z(xyz2+z) k=(yz2) i+(xz2) j+(2xyz+1) k∇f(1,1,2)=(1)(2)2 i+(1)(2)2 j+(2(1)(1)(2)+1) k=4i+4j+5k=⟨4,4,5⟩

Finally, we can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

∇f(x0,y0,z0)⋅⟨x−x0,y−y0,z−z0⟩=0∇f(1,1,2)⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−2⟩=0⟨4,4,5⟩⋅⟨x−1,y−1,z−2⟩=04(x−1)+4(y−1)+5(z−2)=04x+4y+5z−18=0

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,11,1)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $r\cdot ⟨2,-5,4⟩=20.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a point on the plane. If $r=⟨x,y,z⟩,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨2,-5,4⟩ & =20 \\ 2x-5y+4z & =20 \\ 4z & =20-2x+5y \\ z & =5-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $x=2$ and $y=4,$ we get 

$$
z=5-\frac{1}{2}(2)+\frac{5}{4}(4)=9.
$$

So, the point $Q(2,4,9)$ lies on the plane. 

Now, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,4,9⟩-⟨-2,11,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-7,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of a plane, we get a normal vector $n=⟨2,-5,4⟩.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(4)\cdot 2+(-7)\cdot (-5)+8\cdot 4|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|8+35+32|}{\sqrt{4+25+16}} \\  & =\frac{|75|}{\sqrt{45}} \\  & =5\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-11,-8,-4)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $14x+8y-8z=-6.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}14x+8y-8z & =-6 \\ 14(-1)+8(-2)-8z & =-6 \\ -8z & =24 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(-1,-2,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-1,-2,-3⟩-⟨-11,-8,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨10,6,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨14,8,-8⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|10\cdot 14+6\cdot 8+1\cdot (-8)|}{\sqrt{(14)^{2}+{8}^{2}+(-8)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|140+48-8|}{\sqrt{196+64+64}} \\  & =\frac{|\,180\,|}{\sqrt{324}} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-1,11,10)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $-2x-4y+4z=16.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=2$ and $y=3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x-4y+4z & =16 \\ -2(2)-4(3)+4z & =16 \\ 4z & =32 \\ z & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(2,3,8)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,8⟩-⟨-1,11,10⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-8,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-2,-4,4⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|3\cdot (-2)+(-8)\cdot (-4)+(-2)\cdot 4|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-6+32-8|}{\sqrt{4+16+16}} \\  & =\frac{|\,18\,|}{\sqrt{36}} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-1,4,-5)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $-2x+2y+z=6.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+2y+z & =6 \\ -2(1)+2(1)+z & =6 \\ z & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,1,6)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,1,6⟩-⟨-1,4,-5⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-3,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-2,2,1⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|2\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 2+11\cdot 1|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-4-6+11|}{\sqrt{4+4+1}} \\  & =\frac{|1|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Setting $x=2$ and $y=4,$ we get 

$$
z=5-\frac{1}{2}(2)+\frac{5}{4}(4)=9.
$$

So, the point $Q(2,4,9)$ lies on the plane. 

Now, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,4,9⟩-⟨-2,11,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-7,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of a plane, we get a normal vector $n=⟨2,-5,4⟩.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(4)\cdot 2+(-7)\cdot (-5)+8\cdot 4|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|8+35+32|}{\sqrt{4+25+16}} \\  & =\frac{|75|}{\sqrt{45}} \\  & =5\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for x and y into the equation and solve for z. Let's choose x=1 and y=1 (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for z, we get

−2x+2y+z=6−2(1)+2(1)+z=6z=6.

So, we get the point Q(1,1,6) which lies on the plane.

Computing PQ→, we get

PQ→=⟨1,1,6⟩−⟨−1,4,−5⟩=⟨2,−3,11⟩.

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane ax+by+cz=d, the normal vector is n=⟨a,b,c⟩. So, for the plane Π, we have n=⟨−2,2,1⟩.

Finally, the shortest distance from the point P to the plane Π is the absolute value of the scalar projection of PQ→ onto the normal vector of the plane:

d=|compnPQ→|=|PQ→⋅n||n|=|2⋅(−2)+(−3)⋅2+11⋅1|(−2)2+22+12=|−4−6+11|4+4+1=|1|9=13.

question.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,11,1)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $r\cdot ⟨2,-5,4⟩=20.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a point on the plane. If $r=⟨x,y,z⟩,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨2,-5,4⟩ & =20 \\ 2x-5y+4z & =20 \\ 4z & =20-2x+5y \\ z & =5-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $x=2$ and $y=4,$ we get 

$$
z=5-\frac{1}{2}(2)+\frac{5}{4}(4)=9.
$$

So, the point $Q(2,4,9)$ lies on the plane. 

Now, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,4,9⟩-⟨-2,11,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-7,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of a plane, we get a normal vector $n=⟨2,-5,4⟩.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(4)\cdot 2+(-7)\cdot (-5)+8\cdot 4|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|8+35+32|}{\sqrt{4+25+16}} \\  & =\frac{|75|}{\sqrt{45}} \\  & =5\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-11,-8,-4)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $14x+8y-8z=-6.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}14x+8y-8z & =-6 \\ 14(-1)+8(-2)-8z & =-6 \\ -8z & =24 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨-1,-2,-3⟩-⟨-11,-8,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨10,6,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨14,8,-8⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|10\cdot 14+6\cdot 8+1\cdot (-8)|}{\sqrt{(14)^{2}+{8}^{2}+(-8)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|140+48-8|}{\sqrt{196+64+64}} \\  & =\frac{|\,180\,|}{\sqrt{324}} \\  & =10\end{aligned}

Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=2$ and $y=3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x-4y+4z & =16 \\ -2(2)-4(3)+4z & =16 \\ 4z & =32 \\ z & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(2,3,8)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,8⟩-⟨-1,11,10⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-8,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-2,-4,4⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|3\cdot (-2)+(-8)\cdot (-4)+(-2)\cdot 4|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-6+32-8|}{\sqrt{4+16+16}} \\  & =\frac{|\,18\,|}{\sqrt{36}} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Find the shortest distance between the point P(−1,4,−5) and the plane Π with equation −2x+2y+z=6.

a
13
b
23
c
4
d
49
e
3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for x and y into the equation and solve for z. Let's choose x=1 and y=1 (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for z, we get

−2x+2y+z=6−2(1)+2(1)+z=6z=6.

So, we get the point Q(1,1,6) which lies on the plane.

Computing PQ→, we get

PQ→=⟨1,1,6⟩−⟨−1,4,−5⟩=⟨2,−3,11⟩.

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane ax+by+cz=d, the normal vector is n=⟨a,b,c⟩. So, for the plane Π, we have n=⟨−2,2,1⟩.

Finally, the shortest distance from the point P to the plane Π is the absolute value of the scalar projection of PQ→ onto the normal vector of the plane:

d=|compnPQ→|=|PQ→⋅n||n|=|2⋅(−2)+(−3)⋅2+11⋅1|(−2)2+22+12=|−4−6+11|4+4+1=|1|9=13.

questions.problem:
Matt and Andrea each bought $6$ ounces of salted peanuts and $4$ ounces of unsalted peanuts. In total, they bought$\,${{field-1}}
$\,$ounces of peanuts.
questions.worked_solution:
We must write and evaluate an expression representing the total amount of peanuts.

Since each of them bought $6$ ounces of salted peanuts and $4$ ounces of unsalted peanuts, the amount of peanuts they purchased, in ounces, is:

$$
{{6}_{⏟}}_{\text{salted peanuts}}+{{4}_{⏟}}_{\text{unsalted peanuts}}
$$

Since *each* person purchased this amount of peanuts, and there are $2$ people, we must multiply the amount of peanuts by $2.$ Therefore, the total amount of peanuts is:

$$
{{(6+4)}_{⏟}}_{\text{each person}}\times {{2}_{⏟}}_{\text{people}}
$$

To evaluate the expression, we follow the order of operations with parentheses.

First, we perform the operations inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(6+4)\times 2 & =(6+4)\times 2 \\  & =10\times 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply:

$$
10\times 2=20
$$

questions.problem:
Robert bought $3$ pounds of walnuts while Susan bought $\frac{17}{9}$ of a pound of walnuts. How many walnuts did they buy together in total? Express your final answer as a mixed number.

They bought$\,$ 
{{field-1}}
$\,$pounds of walnuts in total.
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the number of walnuts Robert and Susan bought together in total, we have to calculate the following sum:

$$
3+\frac{17}{9}
$$

To add $3$ and $\frac{17}{9},$ we need to express the whole number $3$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of $9.$

First, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{1}
$$

Then we put this fraction over a denominator of $9$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $9:$

$$
\frac{3\times 9}{1\times 9}=\frac{27}{9}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\frac{27}{9}+\frac{17}{9}
$$

To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same:

$$
\frac{27}{9}+\frac{17}{9}=\frac{27+17}{9}=\frac{44}{9}
$$

Expressing our answer as a mixed number, we have

$$
44÷9=4\,\text{R}\,8=4\,\frac{8}{9}.
$$

Therefore, they bought $4\,\frac{8}{9}$ pounds of walnuts.

questions.problem:
Of the $3$ pounds of walnuts that Robert bought, he gave $\frac{3}{5}$ pounds to his granddaughter Sophia. As a mixed number, Robert has{{field-1}}
pounds of walnuts remaining.
questions.worked_solution:
To find out how many walnuts Robert had remaining, we must calculate the difference $3-\frac{3}{5}.$

To subtract $\frac{3}{5}$ from $3,$ we need to express the whole number $3$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of $5.$

First, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{1}
$$

Then, we put this fraction over a denominator of $5$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5:$

$$
\frac{3\times 5}{1\times 5}=\frac{15}{5}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\frac{15}{5}-\frac{3}{5}
$$

To subtract two fractions with like denominators, we subtract the numerators and keep the denominators the same. Therefore:

$$
\frac{15}{5}-\frac{3}{5}=\frac{15-3}{5}=\frac{12}{5}
$$

Finally, we convert to a mixed number:

$$
12÷5=2\,\text{R}\,2=2\,\frac{2}{5}
$$

Therefore, Robert had $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ pounds of walnuts remaining.

questions.worked_solution:
Robert has $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ pounds of walnuts remaining, and Susan has $\frac{17}{9}$ pounds of walnuts.

We cannot compare the fractions directly as they don't have a common denominator.

We can make a common denominator of $5\times 9=45.$

To put $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ over a denominator of $45,$ we first convert to an improper fraction and then multiply the numerator and denominator by $9:$

$$
2\,\frac{2}{5}=\frac{12}{5}=\frac{12\times 9}{5\times 9}=\frac{108}{45}
$$

To put $\frac{17}{9}$ over a denominator of $45,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $5:$

$$
\frac{17}{9}=\frac{17\times 5}{9\times 5}=\frac{85}{45}
$$

We can now compare the fractions $\frac{108}{45}$ and $\frac{85}{45}$ by looking at the numerators only.

Since $108>85,$ the correct statement must be:

$$
\frac{108}{45}>\frac{85}{45}
$$

So, the correct answer is

> "After Sophia takes her walnuts, Robert's remaining amount of walnuts is $>$ than Susan's amount of walnuts because $2\,\frac{2}{5}>\frac{17}{9}.$"

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
To determine the number of walnuts Robert and Susan bought together in total, we have to calculate the following sum:

$$
3+\frac{17}{9}
$$

To add $3$ and $\frac{17}{9},$ we need to express the whole number $3$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of $9.$

First, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{1}
$$

Then we put this fraction over a denominator of $9$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $9:$

$$
\frac{3\times 9}{1\times 9}=\frac{27}{9}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\frac{27}{9}+\frac{17}{9}
$$

To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same:

$$
\frac{27}{9}+\frac{17}{9}=\frac{27+17}{9}=\frac{44}{9}
$$

Expressing our answer as a mixed number, we have

$$
44÷9=4\,\text{R}\,8=4\,\frac{8}{9}.
$$

Therefore, they bought $4\,\frac{8}{9}$ pounds of walnuts.

question.problem:
Robert bought $3$ pounds of walnuts while Susan bought $\frac{17}{9}$ of a pound of walnuts. How many walnuts did they buy together in total? Express your final answer as a mixed number.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        They bought$\,$ 

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\,$pounds of walnuts in total.
question.worked_solution:
To determine the number of walnuts Robert and Susan bought together in total, we have to calculate the following sum:

$$
3+\frac{17}{9}
$$

To add $3$ and $\frac{17}{9},$ we need to express the whole number $3$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of $9.$

First, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{1}
$$

Then we put this fraction over a denominator of $9$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $9:$

$$
\frac{3\times 9}{1\times 9}=\frac{27}{9}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\frac{27}{9}+\frac{17}{9}
$$

To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same:

$$
\frac{27}{9}+\frac{17}{9}=\frac{27+17}{9}=\frac{44}{9}
$$

Expressing our answer as a mixed number, we have

$$
44÷9=4\,\text{R}\,8=4\,\frac{8}{9}.
$$

Therefore, they bought $4\,\frac{8}{9}$ pounds of walnuts.

question.problem:
Of the $3$ pounds of walnuts that Robert bought, he gave $\frac{3}{5}$ pounds to his granddaughter Sophia. As a mixed number, Robert has

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
pounds of walnuts remaining.
question.worked_solution:
To find out how many walnuts Robert had remaining, we must calculate the difference $3-\frac{3}{5}.$

To subtract $\frac{3}{5}$ from $3,$ we need to express the whole number $3$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of $5.$

First, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{1}
$$

Then, we put this fraction over a denominator of $5$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5:$

$$
\frac{3\times 5}{1\times 5}=\frac{15}{5}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\frac{15}{5}-\frac{3}{5}
$$

To subtract two fractions with like denominators, we subtract the numerators and keep the denominators the same. Therefore:

$$
\frac{15}{5}-\frac{3}{5}=\frac{15-3}{5}=\frac{12}{5}
$$

Finally, we convert to a mixed number:

$$
12÷5=2\,\text{R}\,2=2\,\frac{2}{5}
$$

Therefore, Robert had $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ pounds of walnuts remaining.

\frac{15}{5}-\frac{3}{5}
$$

To subtract two fractions with like denominators, we subtract the numerators and keep the denominators the same. Therefore:

$$

$$

Finally, we convert to a mixed number:

$$
12÷5=2\,\text{R}\,2=2\,\frac{2}{5}
$$

Therefore, Robert had $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ pounds of walnuts remaining.

question.worked_solution:
Robert has $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ pounds of walnuts remaining, and Susan has $\frac{17}{9}$ pounds of walnuts.

We cannot compare the fractions directly as they don't have a common denominator.

We can make a common denominator of $5\times 9=45.$

To put $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ over a denominator of $45,$ we first convert to an improper fraction and then multiply the numerator and denominator by $9:$

$$
2\,\frac{2}{5}=\frac{12}{5}=\frac{12\times 9}{5\times 9}=\frac{108}{45}
$$

To put $\frac{17}{9}$ over a denominator of $45,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $5:$

$$
\frac{17}{9}=\frac{17\times 5}{9\times 5}=\frac{85}{45}
$$

We can now compare the fractions $\frac{108}{45}$ and $\frac{85}{45}$ by looking at the numerators only.

Since $108>85,$ the correct statement must be:

$$
\frac{108}{45}>\frac{85}{45}
$$

So, the correct answer is

"After Sophia takes her walnuts, Robert's remaining amount of walnuts is $>$ than Susan's amount of walnuts because $2\,\frac{2}{5}>\frac{17}{9}.$"

question.problem:
Susan ate $\frac{1}{3}$ of the walnuts that she bought. What **exact** amount of walnuts did she eat?

*Remember that Susan bought $\frac{17}{9}$ of a pound of walnuts.*

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        Susan ate$\,$

question.worked_solution:
We know that Susan has $\frac{17}{9}$ of a pound of walnuts.

To calculate the amount that she ate, we need to multiply $\frac{1}{3}$ by $\frac{17}{9}.$

To multiply two fractions, we multiply the numerators, and we multiply the denominators:

$$
\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{17}{9}=\frac{1\times 17}{3\times 9}=\frac{17}{27}.
$$

Therefore, Susan ate $\frac{17}{27}$ of  a pound of walnuts.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: $\int {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}-x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) \\ {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x & =\int ({csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x-\int 1\cdot \text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.$ Rearranging this gives

$$
{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{cot}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}({csc}^{2}⁡x-1)\text{d}x \\  & =(-\operatorname{cot}⁡x-x){|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}]-[-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\frac{\pi }{4}] \\  & =[-0-\frac{\pi }{2}]-[-1-\frac{\pi }{4}] \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}+1+\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.$ Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x+1}{{sec}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a ${tan}^{2}⁡x$ term. So, we can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
{sec}^{2}⁡x-1={tan}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3/2}\frac{3{x}^{2}{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{3/2}\frac{3{x}^{2}{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3/2}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{3/2} \\  & ={(\frac{3}{2})}^{\,3}-{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{27}{8}-1 \\  & =\frac{19}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.$ Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x+1}{{sec}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We use the cosecant-cotangent identity:

$$
1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =-0-(-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: $\int {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}-x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) \\ {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x & =\int ({csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x-\int 1\cdot \text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

∫cot2⁡(π2−x)dx=

a
 cot⁡(π2−x)+x+C
b
 cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
c
 −cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
d
 12cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
e
 −cot⁡(π2−x)+x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the identity 1+cot2⁡θ=csc2⁡θ with θ=π2−x, we get

1+cot2⁡(π2−x)=csc2⁡(π2−x)cot2⁡(π2−x)=csc2⁡(π2−x)−1.

Substituting the above into our integral gives ∫cot2⁡(π2−x)dx=∫(csc2⁡(π2−x)−1)dx=∫csc2⁡(π2−x)dx−∫1⋅dx=cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}-x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) \\ {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x & =\int ({csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)\text{d}x-\int 1\cdot \text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-x)-x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

∫cot2⁡(π2−x)dx=

a
 cot⁡(π2−x)+x+C
b
 cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
c
 −cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
d
 12cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
e
 −cot⁡(π2−x)+x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the identity 1+cot2⁡θ=csc2⁡θ with θ=π2−x, we get

1+cot2⁡(π2−x)=csc2⁡(π2−x)cot2⁡(π2−x)=csc2⁡(π2−x)−1.

Substituting the above into our integral gives ∫cot2⁡(π2−x)dx=∫(csc2⁡(π2−x)−1)dx=∫csc2⁡(π2−x)dx−∫1⋅dx=cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C.

solution.reasoning: Since \cot(\pi/2-x)=\tan x and \tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1, the integral is \tan x-x+C=\cot(\pi/2-x)-x+C, option b. Its derivative equals the integrand. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

$$

Question 1
?

∫cot2⁡(π2−x)dx=

a
 cot⁡(π2−x)+x+C
b
 cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
c
 −cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
d
 12cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C
e
 −cot⁡(π2−x)+x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the identity 1+cot2⁡θ=csc2⁡θ with θ=π2−x, we get

1+cot2⁡(π2−x)=csc2⁡(π2−x)cot2⁡(π2−x)=csc2⁡(π2−x)−1.

Substituting the above into our integral gives ∫cot2⁡(π2−x)dx=∫(csc2⁡(π2−x)−1)dx=∫csc2⁡(π2−x)dx−∫1⋅dx=cot⁡(π2−x)−x+C.

question.name: Question 2
question.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.$ Rearranging this gives

$$
{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{cot}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}({csc}^{2}⁡x-1)\text{d}x \\  & =(-\operatorname{cot}⁡x-x){|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}]-[-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\frac{\pi }{4}] \\  & =[-0-\frac{\pi }{2}]-[-1-\frac{\pi }{4}] \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}+1+\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

b
π2−1

4(π−2)

π−3

4−π
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$

II. $⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$

III. $⟨a,b⟩\in R$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
questions.html:
1.Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product?

Consider the standard Hermitian inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ over C. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. ⟨a,b⟩=⟨b,a⟩― for any a,b∈Cn
  2. ⟨a,αb⟩=α⟨a,b⟩ for any a,b∈Cn and any α∈C
  3. ⟨a,b⟩∈R for any a,b∈Cn

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry.

- Statement II is false. To factor out a constant multiple from the second argument, we must change it to its complex conjugate.

- Statement III is false. The inner product over $C$ is a complex number in general.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ in the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{0}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{0} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=2 \\ {c}_{1}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{c}_{1}=6.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
5\cdot 6+{c}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=-28.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution for the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =6\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+(-28)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}30 \\ 6\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+[\begin{aligned}-28 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to $x$ along a path $C$ is equal to the net change in $x$ between the terminal and initial points:

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x={x}_{2}-{x}_{1},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ is the $x$-coordinate of the terminal point, and ${x}_{1}$ is the $x$-coordinate of the initial point.

In our case, ${x}_{2}=1$ and ${x}_{1}=0.$ Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}x={x}_{2}-{x}_{1}=1-0=1.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The distance between $f(t)=8t-3$ and $g(t)=2t-1$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖8t-3-(2t-1)‖ \\  & =‖6t-2‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨6t-2,6t-2⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨6t-2,6t-2⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6t-2)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(36{t}^{2}-24t+4)\text{d}t \\  & =[12{t}^{3}-12{t}^{2}+4t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(12-12+4)-0 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{4}=2.$

questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q(x)‖ & =‖x‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14177361/assets/04de4ea7dc617be1429c596812ce4f450c2cdaafd8d94d86f75e68a6743acba9.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(z)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y=f(z)=\sqrt{z-1}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,10].$ 

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [1,10],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Therefore, the first component of $r$ is $\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=3{t}^{2}+4,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
1=(0)^{3}+4(0)+C\,⟹\,C=1.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}+4t+1.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1,$ is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=(1)^{3}+4(1)+1=6\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2,$ is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=(2)^{3}+4(2)+1=17\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {17}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =289-36 \\  & =253\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with population mean $\mu .$ Then, the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is given by

$$
\overset{―}{X}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}.
$$

Since $\overset{―}{X}$ is an unbiased estimator of $\mu ,$ we have

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu .
$$

Therefore, since the population mean $\mu =30,$ we have that $\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=30.$

Question 2

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=2 and λ2=1 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where

v1=[51],v2=[10]. Solve the following initial value problem: x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[26]

a
 x(t)=[56]e2t+[280]et
b
 x(t)=[3526]e2t+[−280]et
c
 x(t)=[306]e2t+[−80]et
d
 x(t)=[306]e2t+[−280]et
e
 x(t)=[630]e2t+[280]et

judgments.reasoning: The worked solution resolves the earlier convention uncertainty: MA uses linearity in the first argument and conjugate linearity in the second. I is true by conjugate symmetry. II is false because the scalar becomes its complex conjugate. III is false because inner products of distinct vectors can be nonreal, for example ⟨1,i⟩=−i. The earlier selection, I only, agrees with the worked solution and was graded Correct.

answers.ma_evidence: Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

judgments.reasoning: The eigenvector solution is x(t)=c₁v₁e^{2t}+c₂v₂e^t. The initial condition gives c₁=6 and 5c₁+c₂=2, hence c₂=−28. This produces option d and satisfies both the differential equation and initial condition. The earlier answer matches MA’s worked solution and was graded Correct.

Because dx is an exact differential, the integral equals the terminal x-coordinate minus the initial x-coordinate: 1−0=1. The earlier answer, option e, agrees with MA’s worked solution and was graded Correct.
The difference is f−g=6t−2. Its squared norm is ∫₀¹(6t−2)²dt=12−12+4=4, so the distance is 2. The earlier answer, option e, matches MA’s worked solution and was graded Correct.
Orthogonal transformations preserve norms, so ||Q(x)||=||x||=sqrt(1+4+25)=sqrt(30). The earlier answer, option a, matches MA’s worked solution and was graded Correct.

At each height z, the surface has a circle of radius sqrt(z−1). Pairing x=sqrt(z−1)sin θ with the supplied y=sqrt(z−1)cos θ gives x²+y²=z−1 and traces the full circle. The earlier answer, option c, matches MA’s worked solution and was graded Correct.

answers.ma_evidence: Therefore, the first component of $r$ is $\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

judgments.reasoning: Integrating acceleration with v(0)=1 gives v(t)=t³+4t+1, so v(1)=6 and v(2)=17 m/s. The work is the change in kinetic energy: (1/2)·2·(17²−6²)=253 J. The earlier answer, option e, matches MA’s worked solution and was graded Correct.
By linearity of expectation, E[X̄]=(1/50)∑E[Xᵢ]=(1/50)(50·30)=30. The earlier answer, option d, matches MA’s worked solution and was graded Correct.

answers.ma_evidence: Therefore, since the population mean $\mu =30,$ we have that $\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=30.$

question.problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Solve the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$

question.html:
Question 2

Let A be a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues λ1=2 and λ2=1 corresponding to the eigenvectors v1 and v2 respectively, where

v1=[51],v2=[10]. Solve the following initial value problem: x′(t)=Ax(t),x(0)=[26]

a
 x(t)=[56]e2t+[280]et
b
 x(t)=[3526]e2t+[−280]et
c
 x(t)=[306]e2t+[−80]et
d
 x(t)=[306]e2t+[−280]et
e
 x(t)=[630]e2t+[280]et

solution.reasoning: The solution is x(t)=c₁e^{2t}v₁+c₂e^tv₂. The initial condition gives c₁=6 from the second coordinate and 5c₁+c₂=2, so c₂=−28. Thus x(t)=[30;6]e^{2t}+[−28;0]e^t, which is option d. No MA answer-key or grading evidence is supplied.

a
 (z−1)sin2⁡θ
b
 z−1cos⁡θ
c
 z−1sin⁡θ
d
 (z−1)2sin2⁡θ

question.html:
Question 6

r(z,θ)=⟨__________,z−1cos⁡θ,z⟩

The vector-valued function r(z,θ) above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve y=z−1 by 2π radians about the z-axis for z∈[1,10]. What is the first component of r?

a
 (z−1)sin2⁡θ
b
 z−1cos⁡θ
c
 z−1sin⁡θ
d
 (z−1)2sin2⁡θ
e
 (z−1)sin⁡θ

solution.reasoning: At height z, rotation about the z-axis produces a circle with radius sqrt(z−1), so x²+y²=z−1. With y=sqrt(z−1)cos θ, choosing x=sqrt(z−1)sin θ parametrizes that circle. Thus option c is correct. No MA answer-key or grading evidence is supplied.

question.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $2\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(3{t}^{2}+4)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,m/s$ when $t=0\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$

question.html:
Question 7

A particle P of mass 2kg moves along the x-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is (3t2+4)m/s2, where t≥0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=1m/s when t=0s, calculate the work done by the force between the times t=1s and t=2s.

a
 280J
b
 275J
c
 242J
d
 264J
e
 253J

solution.reasoning: Integrating acceleration and using v(0)=1 gives v(t)=t³+4t+1. Hence v(1)=6 and v(2)=17 m/s. By the work–energy theorem, W=(1/2)m(v(2)²−v(1)²)=17²−6²=253 J, option e. No MA answer-key or grading evidence is supplied.

question.html:
Question 8
A calculator is required to answer the following question.

If X1,X2,…,X50 is a sample of size n=50 drawn from a population with mean μ=30 and variance σ2=9, what is E[X―]?

a
 10
b
 109
c
 103
d
 30
e
 9

solution.reasoning: By linearity of expectation, E[X̄]=(1/50)∑E[Xᵢ]=(1/50)(50·30)=30, option d. The population variance does not affect this expectation. No MA answer-key or grading evidence is supplied.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${(\frac{wt}{2})}^{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{wt}{2})}^{4}=\frac{(wt)^{4}}{{2}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power of product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(wt)^{4}}{{2}^{4}}=\frac{{w}^{4}{t}^{4}}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3wt}{8})}^{2}=\frac{(3wt)^{2}}{{8}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power of product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(3wt)^{2}}{{8}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{{3}^{2}{w}^{2}{t}^{2}}{{8}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{9{w}^{2}{t}^{2}}{64}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{a}{b})}^{3}{(\frac{c}{d})}^{2} & = \\ \frac{(-a)^{3}}{{b}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{c}^{2}}{{d}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{-{a}^{3}}{{b}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{c}^{2}}{{d}^{2}} & = \\ -\frac{{a}^{3}{c}^{2}}{{b}^{3}{d}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4x})}^{2}{(\frac{-2x}{5})}^{3}=\frac{{3}^{2}}{(4x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2x)^{3}}{{5}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we apply the power of product rule and multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{3}^{2}}{(4x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2x)^{3}}{{5}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{{3}^{2}}{{4}^{2}{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2)^{3}{x}^{3}}{{5}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{9}{16{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{-8{x}^{3}}{125} & = \\ \frac{-8\cdot 9{x}^{3}}{16\cdot 125{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the quotient rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-8\cdot 9{x}^{3}}{16\cdot 125{x}^{2}} & = \\ -\frac{9{x}^{3-2}}{2\cdot 125} & = \\ -\frac{9x}{250}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using the Power of Quotient Rule with One Fraction
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\left(\dfrac{2x}{3}\right)^4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{2x}{3})}^{4}=\frac{(2x)^{4}}{{3}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(2x)^{4}}{{3}^{4}} & = \\ \frac{{2}^{4}{x}^{4}}{{3}^{4}} & = \\ \frac{16{x}^{4}}{81} & \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using the Power of Quotient Rule with Two Fractions
canonical_examples.problem: Simplify $\left(\dfrac{y}{2}\right)^3 \left(\dfrac{2y}{3}\right)^2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{y}{2})}^{3}{(\frac{2y}{3})}^{2}=\frac{{y}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}\cdot \frac{(2y)^{2}}{{3}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}\cdot \frac{(2y)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{8}\cdot \frac{{2}^{2}{y}^{2}}{9} & = \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{8}\cdot \frac{4{y}^{2}}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the product rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{3}}{8}\cdot \frac{4{y}^{2}}{9} & = \\ \frac{4{y}^{(3+2)}}{72} & = \\ \frac{4{y}^{5}}{72} & = \\ \frac{{y}^{5}}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **power of quotient rule** states that if we want to raise the quotient $\dfrac{x}{y}$ to some power $n,$ we must raise the numerator and denominator to the power $n$ as follows:

$$
\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)^n=\dfrac{x^n}{y^n}
$$

For example,

$$
\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)^4=\dfrac{x^4}{y^4}.
$$

To see why the power of quotient rule is true, let's take the above example and work it out again the long way. We get the same result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{x}{y})}^{4} & = \\ \frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{x}{y} & = \\ \frac{x\cdot x\cdot x\cdot x}{y\cdot y\cdot y\cdot y} & = \\ \frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The power of quotient rule is just a shortcut for the process above.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}\cdot \frac{(2y)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{8}\cdot \frac{{2}^{2}{y}^{2}}{9} & = \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{8}\cdot \frac{4{y}^{2}}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4x})}^{2}{(\frac{-2x}{5})}^{3}=\frac{{3}^{2}}{(4x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2x)^{3}}{{5}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we apply the power of product rule and multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{3}^{2}}{(4x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2x)^{3}}{{5}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{{3}^{2}}{{4}^{2}{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2)^{3}{x}^{3}}{{5}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{9}{16{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{-8{x}^{3}}{125} & = \\ \frac{-8\cdot 9{x}^{3}}{16\cdot 125{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the quotient rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-8\cdot 9{x}^{3}}{16\cdot 125{x}^{2}} & = \\ -\frac{9{x}^{3-2}}{2\cdot 125} & = \\ -\frac{9x}{250}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{wt}{2})}^{4}=\frac{(wt)^{4}}{{2}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power of product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(wt)^{4}}{{2}^{4}}=\frac{{w}^{4}{t}^{4}}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to (wt2)4?

a
w4t416
b
wt48
c
wt416
d
w4t48
e
w4t42
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

(wt2)4=(wt)424

Then, we apply the power of product rule:

(wt)424=w4t416

question.name: Question 2
question.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3wt}{8})}^{2}=\frac{(3wt)^{2}}{{8}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power of product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(3wt)^{2}}{{8}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{{3}^{2}{w}^{2}{t}^{2}}{{8}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{9{w}^{2}{t}^{2}}{64}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3wt}{8})}^{2}=\frac{(3wt)^{2}}{{8}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the power of product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(3wt)^{2}}{{8}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{{3}^{2}{w}^{2}{t}^{2}}{{8}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{9{w}^{2}{t}^{2}}{64}\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
We apply the power of quotient rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{a}{b})}^{3}{(\frac{c}{d})}^{2} & = \\ \frac{(-a)^{3}}{{b}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{c}^{2}}{{d}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{-{a}^{3}}{{b}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{c}^{2}}{{d}^{2}} & = \\ -\frac{{a}^{3}{c}^{2}}{{b}^{3}{d}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Power of Quotient Rule with Two Fractions
last_observation.worked_solution:
We apply the power of quotient rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{a}{b})}^{3}{(\frac{c}{d})}^{2} & = \\ \frac{(-a)^{3}}{{b}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{c}^{2}}{{d}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{-{a}^{3}}{{b}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{c}^{2}}{{d}^{2}} & = \\ -\frac{{a}^{3}{c}^{2}}{{b}^{3}{d}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Using the Power of Quotient Rule with Two Fractions

solution.reasoning: The odd power preserves the negative sign: (-a/b)^3 = -a^3/b^3. Also, (c/d)^2 = c^2/d^2. Multiplying gives -a^3c^2/(b^3d^2), matching option e, with b and d nonzero. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns a different expression.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.worked_solution:
We apply the power of quotient rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{a}{b})}^{3}{(\frac{c}{d})}^{2} & = \\ \frac{(-a)^{3}}{{b}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{c}^{2}}{{d}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{-{a}^{3}}{{b}^{3}}\cdot \frac{{c}^{2}}{{d}^{2}} & = \\ -\frac{{a}^{3}{c}^{2}}{{b}^{3}{d}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
We apply the power of quotient rule and simplify:

$$

question.knowledge_point: Using the Power of Quotient Rule with Two Fractions

solution.reasoning: Applying the power of quotient rule gives (s/2)^4(4/t)^2 = (s^4/16)(16/t^2) = s^4/t^2 for t nonzero, matching option d. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the supplied worked example solves a different expression.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.worked_solution:
We apply the power of quotient rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{s}{2})}^{4}{(\frac{4}{t})}^{2} & = \\ \frac{{s}^{4}}{{2}^{4}}\cdot \frac{{4}^{2}}{{t}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{{s}^{4}}{16}\cdot \frac{16}{{t}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{16{s}^{4}}{16{t}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{{s}^{4}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4x})}^{2}{(\frac{-2x}{5})}^{3}=\frac{{3}^{2}}{(4x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2x)^{3}}{{5}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we apply the power of product rule and multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{3}^{2}}{(4x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2x)^{3}}{{5}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{{3}^{2}}{{4}^{2}{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2)^{3}{x}^{3}}{{5}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{9}{16{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{-8{x}^{3}}{125} & = \\ \frac{-8\cdot 9{x}^{3}}{16\cdot 125{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the quotient rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-8\cdot 9{x}^{3}}{16\cdot 125{x}^{2}} & = \\ -\frac{9{x}^{3-2}}{2\cdot 125} & = \\ -\frac{9x}{250}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

(34x)2(−2x5)3=

a
−9x125
b
1259x2
c
−9x250
d
−2503
e
3125x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

(34x)2(−2x5)3=32(4x)2⋅(−2x)353

Next, we apply the power of product rule and multiply:

32(4x)2⋅(−2x)353=3242x2⋅(−2)3x353=916x2⋅−8x3125=−8⋅9x316⋅125x2

Finally, we apply the quotient rule and simplify:

−8⋅9x316⋅125x2=−9x3−22⋅125=−9x250

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Power of Quotient Rule with Two Fractions
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we apply the power of quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4x})}^{2}{(\frac{-2x}{5})}^{3}=\frac{{3}^{2}}{(4x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2x)^{3}}{{5}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we apply the power of product rule and multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{3}^{2}}{(4x)^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2x)^{3}}{{5}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{{3}^{2}}{{4}^{2}{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{(-2)^{3}{x}^{3}}{{5}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{9}{16{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{-8{x}^{3}}{125} & = \\ \frac{-8\cdot 9{x}^{3}}{16\cdot 125{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we apply the quotient rule and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-8\cdot 9{x}^{3}}{16\cdot 125{x}^{2}} & = \\ -\frac{9{x}^{3-2}}{2\cdot 125} & = \\ -\frac{9x}{250}\end{aligned}
$$
